title: Survival and Time-Average Growth Define the Function of Everyday Acts

detail.title: Survival and Time-Average Growth Define the Function of Everyday Acts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical study that involved no human participants, patients or animals.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract: People judge everyday acts by their form, by the satisfaction they bring or by their expected pay-off. That the same outlay can be consumption or investment is long established, but separating the two in a given act has been called formidable. Here we show that, for an agent whose base (body, skills, resources and trust) depreciates and whose gains and losses compound multiplicatively, comparing the agent's time-average growth under an act, under the same act with its yield disconnected, and under inaction separates what the act returns from what it costs: its productive from its consumptive function. Leaving a return, outperforming inaction, maintaining the base and satisfying a survival constraint are nested conditions, each required for the next and none ensuring it. Because survival requires positive growth, inaction is never admissible under depreciation, and survival sets a floor under activity as well as a limit on risk. One-off changes shift the level of the base, not its growth, and weigh most near the survival threshold. Applied to child-rearing, the comparison identifies a productive activity whose net advantage can be negative for the parents who bear its costs, and it yields testable predictions for debates on fertility, generative artificial intelligence and screen use.

title: Value Positioning & Architecture (VPA): Constructing Bulletproof Market Differentiation

detail.title: Value Positioning & Architecture (VPA): Constructing Bulletproof Market Differentiation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and lead strategist of Vandabon and has commercial interests in the implementation of the Vandabon 360° Growth Ecosystem.

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Background. Industrial and complex B2B suppliers frequently possess differentiated engineering capability yet compete through cost-plus bids, line-item comparisons, and concessions. This paper develops Value Positioning & Architecture (VPA), a managerial protocol for translating distinctive capability into a defensible market position, an integrated offer, and disciplined commercial governance. Diagnostic Crisis. The central problem is not necessarily an objectively excessive price. It is often a failure to make economic consequences, evidence, delivery boundaries, and alternatives legible to the buying organization. This failure produces four mutually reinforcing conditions: commodity comparison and negative-margin bidding; scarce technical capacity consumed by unqualified prospects; inability to sell integrated, high-value interventions; and procurement-led concessions coupled with asymmetric contractual risk. Economic Value Architecture. VPA connects customer economics to offer design and price. It estimates incremental value against a credible counterfactual, discounts uncertainty and attribution, distinguishes value from supplier cost, and sets a negotiated share within a viable buyer-surplus zone. A transparent total cost of inaction (TCOI) model makes delay and non-adoption explicit without presenting uncertain benefits as guarantees. Strategic Positioning Protocol. The protocol has four phases: (1) extract and triple-validate proprietary differentiation; (2) architect integrated offers and model TCOI; (3) establish authority before first executive contact and conduct diagnostic selling; and (4) govern price through approval rules and reciprocal trades rather than unilateral discounting. Practical & Managerial Implications. VPA is not a slogan, premium-price license, or substitute for operational competence. It depends on evidence quality, delivery capacity, executive sponsorship, deal-level economics, and reviewable governance. Within Vandabon, DRA supplies leakage diagnostics, VPA defines economically coherent positioning and boundaries, and SSIO operationalizes the promise through connected sales and delivery processes.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how financial markets can insure households against the risks created by labor-displacing technologies. We develop a two-period general-equilibrium model in which technological progress raises output and firm profits but increases workers' labor-income risk. These effects create opposing forces in asset prices. The abundance force occurs when technological progress raises consumption, lowering marginal utility in the same states in which firm cash flows are high and therefore reducing the value of those cash flows. In contrast, the displacement force raises workers' willingness to pay for equity that pays off when displacement risk is high. Workers may value this equity more highly than its few initial shareholders do. Applied to frontier AI labs, the model shows a public offering can raise the labs' market value, partially insure workers, and improve welfare.

detail.abstract: This study examined how Starbucks Philippines maintains its global brand standards while adapting the preferences, expectations, and competitive conditions of the local coffee market. The study focuses on the company global brand identity, store environment, customer service, product presentation, digital services, and customer experiences. The study uses a qualitative content analysis on research design based on the publicly secondary sources, including academic journals, official Starbucks Philippines, industry reports, and business articles published from 2021 to 2026. The collected information was reviewed, categorized, and analyzed according to themes related to global brand identity, and local market adaptation. The findings highlight that Starbucks maintains its recognizable global brand identity through consistent visual presentation, store atmosphere, product quality, and customer service experience, while also demonstrate their effort to respond to the needs of Filipino consumers. Furthermore, the study recognizes that Starbucks continues to maintain a strong position in the Philippine Coffee market while facing increasing competition from local and international coffee brands. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that Starbucks Philippines demonstrates how a multinational coffee company can preserve its global brand identity while responding to the local market conditions through product quality, and customer experience.

title: The Wealth of Algorithms: Generative AI, Jobs and Inequality in a Global Dynamic CGE Model

detail.title: The Wealth of Algorithms: Generative AI, Jobs and Inequality in a Global Dynamic CGE Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: This paper models how generative artificial intelligence (AI) affects jobs, wages and inequality across the world economy. Few doubt that it will change the economy; what nobody yet knows is how. Workers, firms and governments want to know whose jobs and pay will change, who will capture the gains and which countries will come out ahead, well before the evidence can tell them. This paper does not try to forecast that future. Its contribution is a quantitative framework for understanding what drives AI's economic effects, what they depend on, and what follows for policy. We add AI to a global dynamic computable general equilibrium (CGE) model that tracks production, trade, investment and employment year by year to 2040 in 23 regions. AI does some tasks inside each occupation and makes workers more productive in others. When AI does a task, we start from a 27% saving on its labour cost, the average Acemoglu (2025) draws from two workplace experiments. We run a central scenario and 68 alternatives that vary how fast and how widely AI is adopted, what it costs, how far it replaces rather than helps workers and how labour markets adjust. How cheap and capable AI becomes, and how widely firms adopt it, decide the size of the gain: by 2040 world GDP ends about 1% to 15% above a path without AI in our main scenarios (about 7% in the central case). It reaches about 35% in an extreme case where AI becomes 30% a year more efficient (15 to 25% if AI keeps improving but more slowly over time). Most of the gain goes to owners of capital in almost every scenario. Who shares in it depends on who owns capital and on the extent to which AI replaces rather than helps workers. In the central case capital's share of world income rises by about 4 points, clerks' real pay ends roughly 13 to 22% below the no-AI path in the large economies, and within rich economies the Gini coefficient of household income rises by about 2 to 3.5 points. If job losses last, the world gain against the no-AI baseline in 2040 is 5.4% against 6.8%, and labour income falls further everywhere. Based on these results, we then test several illustrative AI policies to see how they change the outcomes and their distributional effects. Each does a different job: support for changing jobs mainly protects workers' pay, keeping AI cheap mainly protects output, and only sharing AI's capital income narrows inequality noticeably. The policies are illustrative and largely unfunded in the model, so their gains are likely inflated.

title: How Paywall Suspensions Expand Digital Access: Evidence from Branded News App Downloads
affiliations: University of Missouri at Saint Louis

detail.title: How Paywall Suspensions Expand Digital Access: Evidence from Branded News App Downloads

affiliations.org_name: University of Missouri at Saint Louis
affiliations.preferred_name: University of Missouri at Saint Louis

detail.abstract: Newspapers suspend paywalls during major news events to ensure public access to vital information. Yet, the policy implications of such suspensions for digital equity and news access remain underexplored. This study investigates whether and under what conditions temporary paywall suspensions can enhance the adoption of branded mobile news apps—a durable and potentially more inclusive form of digital engagement. Using 6,396 daily news app download observations across 25 paywall suspensions by 12 U.S. newspapers during 13 major events, we estimate the heterogeneous and time-varying effects of paywall suspensions on app downloads through a Bayesian panel causal inference framework. We find that paywall suspension increases app downloads substantially. The impact varies, however, with greater effects for more important news events, newspapers with larger audiences, and geographically relevant suspensions. Importantly, the effectiveness of geo-relevant suspensions depends on the newspaper audience size: they significantly boost app downloads for smaller newspapers but have little effect for larger ones. This pattern suggests that small newspapers benefit more from locally targeted access policies. Our findings have implications for both policymakers concerned with digital access and publishers making strategic paywall suspension decisions during critical events.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper examines how the tender-based purchasing models of the Nordic state
alcohol monopolies – Systembolaget (Sweden), Vinmonopolet (Norway) and Alko (Finland)
– shape the market-entry requirements facing French wine exporters.
Design/methodology/approach: The study is a qualitative, desk-based comparative case
study. It draws on the monopolies’ published supplier guidance, purchasing-process
documentation, assortment plans and sustainability requirements, supplemented by an
illustrative coding of 17 French-eligible Vinmonopolet tenders published in 2026 and by
academic literature on alcohol policy, public procurement and wine export strategy.
Findings: Although the three monopolies differ in tender frequency, assortment architecture
and alternative listing routes, they share a specification-led procurement logic. Market access
depends less on informal importer relationships than on tender intelligence, precise product-
market matching, compliant documentation, credible supply capacity, landed-cost modelling
and verifiable sustainability credentials. The illustrative coding shows French wines securing
permanent basic-range listings where they match narrowly specified tenders, concentrated in
mid-priced and premium segments.
Research limitations/implications: The study relies on public documents and a single-
monopoly, single-year tender coding; it cannot observe confidential scoring, importer margins or post-launch sales performance.
Practical implications: The paper proposes a capability-based market-entry framework
covering regulatory readiness, tender intelligence, specification matching, commercial
modelling, sustainability readiness, route-to-market sequencing and importer partnership.
Originality: The paper combines the wine export strategy and public procurement literatures
to show how monopoly retail structures alter the logic of international market entry.

title: The Four Foundations of Entrepreneurial Customer Insight: An Integrated and Developmental Framework for Honest Idea Evaluation

detail.title: The Four Foundations of Entrepreneurial Customer Insight: An Integrated and Developmental Framework for Honest Idea Evaluation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the author and publisher of books and working papers cited in this article, including Is It Really a Great Idea?, and is the founder of Innovation Culture Institute LLC, which publishes and distributes related educational materials. The author declares no other competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual and practitioner-oriented paper did not involve human subjects, patient data, participant recruitment, or experimental research requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Entrepreneurs can complete customer interviews, document observations, and conduct experiments without developing an adequate understanding of the people they intend to serve. A procedure can be followed while its purpose is defeated: customers are interpreted through the founder’s preferences, inquiry stops at a convenient explanation, and evidence is used to defend rather than evaluate the idea. This paper proposes an integrated framework for understanding the evaluator behind the evaluation.

The framework comprises four foundations: Cognitive Empathy, the capacity to understand customers through their own priorities and circumstances; Genuine Care, a commitment to improving their outcomes independently of acceptance of a preferred solution; Extreme Curiosity, sustained investigation beyond surface explanations; and Intellectual Honesty, the willingness to let evidence govern conclusions and decisions. The central proposition is that these foundations contribute in complementary ways. Weakness in one creates vulnerabilities that strength in the others may not fully compensate for. This proposition concerns customer-centered discovery and evaluation, not a proven formula for entrepreneurial success.

Drawing on entrepreneurship, psychology, and management research, the paper distinguishes established findings from its proposed integration. Contrasting behavioral portraits illustrate stronger and weaker expressions without assigning permanent personality labels or numerical scores. Developmental practices, feedback, and process safeguards link vulnerability recognition to practical responses. The paper presents research propositions and discusses limitations concerning complementarity, development, and the separate assessment of customer understanding, customer benefit, and decision quality.

title: Markdowns to Reduce Food Waste and Their Impact on Retail Brand Image
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst - Department of Operations and Information Management and Boston University

detail.title: Markdowns to Reduce Food Waste and Their Impact on Retail Brand Image

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by internal university research funds.

affiliations.org_name: University of Massachusetts Amherst - Department of Operations and Information Management
affiliations.preferred_name: University of Massachusetts Amherst - Department of Operations and Information Management

detail.abstract:
Problem Definition: Marking down surplus food products is an effective way for retailers to reduce food waste in the supply chain, yet many hesitate to use this strategy due to concerns that discounts may damage their brand image. This hesitation not only exacerbates environmental impact but also leads retailers to miss out on potential revenue gains. This study examines whether discounting surplus food negatively affects consumers' perceptions of retailers. 

Methodology/Results: We use complementary in-store and online experiments. The in-store experiment, conducted at an independent U.S. grocery store, shows that-contrary to retailers' concerns-markdowns on surplus food do not harm consumers' evaluations of the retailer. Moreover, the framing of the discount matters: when discount signs use environmental language (e.g., "sustainable choice" or "zero-waste choice"), retailer evaluation scores increase relative to a no-discount control condition. Additionally, discounting surplus food does not change shoppers' basket size. We extend the analysis to an online experiment to assess whether consumer responses vary across countries, with samples from France, Germany, South Africa, the U.K., and the U.S. Results across all countries except South Africa mirror the in-store findings: no discount type reduces retailer brand-image scores, and "zero-waste" framing generally increases them. South African consumers, however, appear to react negatively to the term "zero-waste." 

Managerial Implications: Our findings suggest that retailers can use markdowns to reduce food waste without damaging their brand image. They also underscore that retailers should consider cultural differences when designing food-surplus exit strategies and discount-framing practices.

title: The Agentic Oversight Tax: Supervising AI Agents Has a Cognitive, Affective and Organizational Cost that Must Be Measured

detail.title: The Agentic Oversight Tax: Supervising AI Agents Has a Cognitive, Affective and Organizational Cost that Must Be Measured

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Olivier Oullier is a Professor at the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), co-founder and CEO of Inclusive Brains, Chief AI Scientist of Biotech Dental Group and Chairman of its AI Institute. He is a shareholder and the former President of EMOTIV.

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

affiliations.org_name: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations.preferred_name: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: This position paper argues that human supervision of AI agents imposes a composite cognitive, affective and organizational cost that none of the human factors or occupational measurement frameworks reviewed here jointly captures. We introduce the Agentic Oversight Tax (AOT) as the combined burden that falls on a human supervisor when the operating characteristics of one or more AI agents exceed the neurocognitive capacities of the person overseeing them. AOT is made of four measurable pillars: monitoring time, handoff repair events, audit production effort and recovery effort under staged failures. We ground each pillar in supervision failures documented between 2024 and 2026 and we compare them with the failure categories of the MAST taxonomy, which records agent failures without any data on the human supervisor. We argue, pending empirical validation, that AOT is distinct from seven adjacent frameworks because each of them either excludes by definition or names without measuring three phenomena: attribution burden, accountability gap and skill atrophy. The pillars can be assessed at three levels of instrumentation: system telemetry, periodic self-report and neurophysiological sensing. Any AOT instrument must also correct for attribution bias associated with dual-process accounts of cognition. A pre-registered meta-analysis of 100+ experiments comparing human-AI combinations with humans alone and AI alone, shows that, in decision-making tasks, though not in content creation ones, human-AI combinations performed worse on average than the best of humans or AI solutions alone. Governance frameworks such as the EU AI Act mandate human oversight without measuring its cost, so they cannot verify whether the oversight they require remains feasible at agent speed and scale. We propose AOT as a measurement construct for that cost and call on the machine learning community to report it in deployment evaluations, to treat supervisability as a design requirement and to develop thresholds that indicate when oversight has become nominal.

title: When the Manager Builds the Tool: AI-Assisted Decision Support, Margin Visibility and Advertising Efficiency in a Small E-commerce Firm

detail.title: When the Manager Builds the Tool: AI-Assisted Decision Support, Margin Visibility and Advertising Efficiency in a Small E-commerce Firm

detail.abstract: Generative AI has lowered the cost of building custom business software to the point where a single manager can do it. Most evidence on AI and decision tools comes from large organisations, and little is known about small firms in which the manager builds the tool himself. This paper studies one such case: a UK private-label home-goods seller on Amazon, mainly in textiles" vertically integrated with its own factory, whose manager built a decision-support system with AI coding assistants. The system went live in mid-October 2026. It combines rule-based logic with calls to a language model and, for the first time, places margin per unit beside sales, advertising and inventory data. I compare the four weeks after go-live with the four weeks before and difference this change against the same calendar windows in 2025. Relative to the prior year, return on ad spend rose by 0.92 and total advertising cost of sales fell by 2.9 percentage points. Within 2026, the share of advertising spend allocated to weak campaigns fell from 9% to 1%, a decline that holds across alternative definitions of a weak campaign. The evidence comes from one firm over one month and is preliminary. It suggests that AI-built tools can give small firms decision capabilities that were previously limited to large ones, and that the earliest gains appear in fast-moving decisions such as advertising.

detail.abstract: Stock-outs are known to cost retailers more than the sale that is missed, but evidence from online marketplaces comes mainly from practitioner reports that disagree with one another. This paper measures what happens to traffic and sales after stock-outs for a small, vertically integrated home-textiles seller on Amazon, using daily inventory records for 45 products and monthly traffic data from August 2025 to February 2026. In a monthly panel with product and month fixed effects, each week out of stock lowers that month's sessions by about 17% and units sold by about 27%. In the following month, sessions return to their normal level, but conversion remains about 13% lower. An episode-level analysis of 17 restocks shows that sales in the first week after a restock are about two-thirds of their normal level under three alternative baselines; recovery after that is less precisely measured. The results suggest that, for a small marketplace seller, the lasting cost of a stock-out lies less in lost visibility than in lower conversion once the product returns.

detail.abstract: We study how a platform can use cost-effective subsidies to incentivize driver supply when there is a shortterm demand surge. A structural model is developed to capture the heterogeneity in driver supply, and a field experiment of driver subsidization is used to identify the income sensitivity of drivers. We find a large variation in expected earnings and work costs across drivers and hours of the day. Counterfactual analyses reveal that, because drivers are income-insensitive, a uniform constant subsidy policy will incur a heavy profit loss for the platform. However, personalized and dynamic subsidy policies can substantially reduce the loss. The former policy provides higher subsidies to those who have high abilities and low work costs, while the latter offers higher subsidies to those who work longer hours. Consequently, the increase in total driver supply primarily comes from intensive margin, i.e. active drivers increasing work hours given the subsidy. This is because these drivers are flexible in their work schedule, a phenomenon unique to the gig economy.

title: Historical Performance Evaluation of a Mechanical 15-Minute Opening Range Breakout Strategy in the XAU/USD Market During the New York Session (2016-2025)

detail.title: Historical Performance Evaluation of a Mechanical 15-Minute Opening Range Breakout Strategy in the XAU/USD Market During the New York Session (2016-2025)

detail.abstract: This study evaluates the historical performance of a fixed, fully mechanical 15-minute Opening Range Breakout (ORB) strategy applied to the XAU/USD market during the New York trading session. The analysis uses one-minute BID and ASK price data obtained from Dukascopy Bank SA, covering the period from 3 January 2016 to 31 December 2025. The opening range is defined by the 9:30-9:45 AM New York time candle. A trade is triggered when a subsequent 15-minute candle closes beyond the opening range, with entry occurring at the next available one-minute opening price. The strategy uses the opposite boundary of the opening range as its stop-loss and a fixed take-profit level of 2.3 times the initial risk. Separate BID and ASK prices are used for trade execution to incorporate the bid-ask spread. The backtest produced 2,457 completed trades over the ten-year sample period. The overall win rate was 29.51%, while the average net expectancy was-0.02989R per trade, resulting in a cumulative net outcome of-73.44R. Statistical testing found no significant difference between the observed mean expectancy and zero (t =-0.9793, p = 0.3274). The 95% confidence interval for mean expectancy ranged from-0.08971R to 0.02993R. The findings indicate that the tested ORB configuration did not demonstrate positive average performance over the examined period. These results provide a historical assessment of the specified strategy under the stated execution assumptions and highlight the importance of evaluating trading strategies through long-term empirical testing and statistical analysis.

title: Fractured Innovation: Institutional Sequencing Failures In Drug Development
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - School of Law and DePaul University - College of Law

detail.title: Fractured Innovation: Institutional Sequencing Failures In Drug Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: UCLA School of Law and DePaul Law School

affiliations.org_name: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - School of Law
affiliations.preferred_name: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - School of Law

detail.abstract:
Innovation law scholarship has long focused on a singular goal: how to design discrete incentives to optimize the outputs of innovation.  In the drug development context, this focus translates into an effort to fine-tune patent strength, regulatory exclusivity thresholds, and reimbursement schemes.  This Article argues that this focus rests on a mistaken premise: that incentives for innovation can be optimized in isolation, within the four corners of the individual institutions responsible for administering them.  But drug innovation does not take place within a single institutional boundary.  Rather, it unfolds through a sequence of public and private actors, the NIH, PTO, FDA, CMS and private insurance, whose decisions impact innovation outputs at specific time points.  The central challenge in drug development is therefore not just incentive design but coordination-in-time across this institutional sequence.

We reconceptualize drug development as a relay in which innovation failures take place at the handoffs between institutions.  We identify two types of systemic effects—regulatory spillovers and mission gaps—that emerge from this relay structure.  Regulatory spillovers refer to unintended consequences that flow to downstream, later-in-time actors from upstream institutional choices.  For example, FDA reliance on lower-quality evidence to spur investment in difficult disease areas leaves insurers and clinicians without the data needed for coverage and treatment decisions.  Regulatory spillovers are sticky: downstream actors often lack the ability to reverse or mitigate their effects.  Mission gaps capture instances where no institutional actor in the sequence is tasked with essential innovation functions.  For example, many potentially life-saving drugs languish because no single institution is responsible for shepherding the most promising among them from conception to commercialization.  Crucially, regulatory spillovers and mission gaps generate second-order innovation failures that are undertheorized in the incentives literature: the persistent lack of clinically meaningful data about drugs, and the early death of promising therapies.

These coordination-in-time failures cannot be solved by fine-tuning incentive schemes within individual institutions.  Instead, effective innovation policy requires attention to how incentives interact across institutions and how their effects depend on the timing of institutional decisions. Drawing on polycentric governance theory and using the pandemic-era public-private ACTIV consortium as an empirical anchor, this Article instead proposes an earlier-stage, structured coordination track for high-need drugs that aligns incentives and institutional commitments before key development decisions become fixed. The proposed solution brings relevant institutions together early and sustains their collaboration throughout the drug development process. This approach preserves institutional autonomy while creating binding commitments on key features—such as clinical trial design and funding streams—across agencies and private actors early in the drug development pipeline.

The Article develops the concept of coordination-in-time in the context of drug development, but its conceptual framework extends beyond drug innovation institutions.  More broadly, institutional sequencing represents an underappreciated source of administrative failure in complex regulatory regimes, one that merits deeper analysis across different institutional environments.

detail.abstract: This working paper revisits and substantially reframes a 2019 Master's thesis on social entrepreneurship and postconflict rehabilitation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). It develops the concept of Rehabilitative Social Entrepreneurship (ReSE) to explain how community-based entrepreneurial activity may contribute to the recovery of people whose livelihoods, social networks, capabilities and sense of agency have been damaged by armed conflict. The argument is that social entrepreneurship is not rehabilitative simply because it creates income or provides services. Its rehabilitative potential depends on whether affected people participate meaningfully in identifying needs, mobilising resources, governing collective activity and controlling the benefits generated. The empirical foundation is the original qualitative case study conducted in eastern DRC, principally in Bukavu, Goma and Ituri, and involving four organisations: Synergie Simama, YES DRC, Kivu Entrepreneurs and CEDERU. The thesis reports 100 targeted informants and 85 completed questionnaires, alongside interviews with communitybased organisers and interpretive analysis of participants' accounts. Reported findings point to interconnected constraints-income and employment deprivation, inadequate skills, weakened networks, physical impairment and psychosocial distress-and to the perceived value of training, work opportunities, income, networks and community participation. The paper preserves these historical findings while identifying inconsistencies in the original responserate and demographic tables that limit the precision of quantitative interpretation. The paper updates the conceptual and contextual discussion using contemporary research on entrepreneurship in postconflict settings and the International Labour Organization's definition of the social and solidarity economy. It also situates the 2019 field evidence against the continuing and renewed displacement and insecurity documented in 2025-2026. This update is contextual, not a new field survey: no new interviews or outcome measurements are claimed. The paper proposes a four-dimensional ReSE framework-opportunity and innovation; resource mobilisation and social capital; survivor agency and participatory governance; and multidimensional rehabilitationtogether with safeguards against exclusion, elite capture, conflict sensitivity and the substitution of public obligations by under-resourced community organisations.

detail.abstract: While traditional hub capacity planning models optimize effectively for quantitative inputs, they often fail to digest qualitative business context. We propose a novel framework where a large language model (LLM) agent iteratively proposes hub capacity decisions guided by natural-language business context descriptions. The key mechanism is a chain-of-thought reasoning protocol: the LLM constructs a structured decision table that maps each contextual item to specific capacity adjustments based on the implied direction and magnitude of changes. The new capacity decision is then validated through a feedback loop with an optimization model, which provides routing-based performance metrics to guide the agent's selection. On a real-world 13-hub freight network in the southeastern US, our framework achieves a 2.8% optimality gap relative to the hidden ground-truth, a significant improvement over the 11.0% gap produced by the traditional optimization model without textual business inputs. This demonstrates that LLMs can serve as a contextual bridge, integrating qualitative business insights into Operations Research workflows.

detail.abstract: The increasing reliance on machine learning relies on data that are often disaggregated and distributed within organisations and between businesses, devices and jurisdictions, and that cannot be aggregated without legal, ethical or commercial cost. To balance the need for data utility and privacy, federated learning (FL) and arcinformed privacy preserving machine learning (PPML) techniques have been proposed. The current state of the field from 2019-2025 is presented along with some of the foundational work if it facilitates the understanding. Presenting the material in a structured format, it combines evidence about four major technical areas: federated optimisation, differential privacy, secure aggregation and secure computation and also about the attacks that drive them: membership inference, model inversion, gradient leakage and poisoning. The authors reviewed found that data locality does not ensure privacy: Sharing updates can be "inverted", meaning that updates to some data sources can be repackaged to update other sources, and secure aggregation can be compromised by a malicious coordinator. There are formal protections, each with measurable costs if taken to loads of accuracy, communication (or computation), and the variability of the data and the number of participants, each of which is unevenly distributed around scale, data mix, and participants. Healthcare and mobile computing literature demonstrate that federated systems can achieve the same or very close performance to central systems in certain situations, but reports of privacy parameters and models of threats vary. We sketch a framework for selecting protections from a several layers perspective that considers malicious threats and outline a series of open problems (auditing privacy guarantees, privacy defensibility with respect to robustness, governance for LFSMs, and standardising evaluation). The results will guide researchers and practitioners in designing federated systems that can have clear and verifiable privacy claims that are commensurate with the risk.

detail.abstract: Two stocks with the same past return may have risen by gradually absorbing news or on noise that later reverts. We separate them with coherence, a wavelet semblance measure of whether a stock's recent return swings have advanced steadily or reversed. Coherent momentum earns 0.74% per month in equal-weighted portfolios of non-microcap stocks from 1931 to 2024, beating conventional momentum by 0.10% and fragile, low-coherence momentum by 0.19%. The premium arises in the first month after formation, a horizon at which existing path measures such as trend clarity are weakest. Coherence does not predict news. It predicts how prices absorb news, and the fragility discount is concentrated in months without earnings announcements.

detail.abstract: This study evaluated the energy efficiency and financial implications of the energy-conservation measures implemented by the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) under Revenue Memorandum Order (RMO) No. 7-2026. Specifically, it examined changes in electricity, water, and fuel consumption equivalents and related expenditures, and assessed whether the observed changes indicated greater reductions in the BIR than in the Department of Finance (DOF). The study employed a quantitative, descriptive, archival, and quasi-experimental comparative approach using secondary financial, administrative, and operational data from the BIR and relevant DOF records for January to June of 2024, 2025, and 2026. Historical utility and fuel price references were applied to disbursement records to estimate implied resource-consumption equivalents, while historical-benchmark comparisons, exploratory statistical tests, and difference-indifferences analysis were used to examine changes. Findings showed estimated reductions of 22.63% in electricity consumption equivalent, 9.85% in fuel equivalent, and 0.41% in water equivalent relative to the 2024-2025 historical benchmarks. The electricity difference was statistically significant (p = 0.0000393), whereas the fuel (p = 0.400814) and water (p = 0.945028) differences were not. However, the comparative analysis did not establish a statistically significant greater reduction in the BIR than in the DOF. The comparative null hypothesis was therefore not rejected, and net savings attributable to RMO No. 7-2026 were not established. Since the estimates were derived from aggregate disbursements and external price references rather than direct metering, the results support descriptive assessment but do not demonstrate a causal policy effect. The study underscores the need for facilitylevel electricity monitoring, actual water-meter readings, transaction-level fuel records, and longer-term evaluation to strengthen evidence-based resource management and determine genuine net savings.

title: Strategic Returned Part Recovery: A Decision Model for Reuse, Remanufacturing, and Recycling
affiliations: Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE), Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE) and Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE)

detail.title: Strategic Returned Part Recovery: A Decision Model for Reuse, Remanufacturing, and Recycling

declarations.funderStatement: This publication is part of the project ADD-reAM with file number NWA.1766.24.015 of the NWA-ORC research program which is (partly) financed by the Dutch Research Council (NWO).

detail.abstract: Customers may return components after use because they have failed or are no longer needed. These components can be recycled, remanufactured, or sometimes even reused as is. Remanufacturing to restore a component's condition can be done by additive or conventional manufacturing. Deciding to what level to restore a component involves a trade-off between recovered value and restoration cost. However, existing decision models treat remanufacturing as a predetermined recovery option with an associated fixed cost and overlook this trade-off. We develop an economic decision model to evaluate direct reuse, remanufacturing, and recycling on a common net profit basis. Each returned component is represented by two conditions: functional service condition and marketable non-functional condition. These conditions capture functional capability and non-functional attributes affecting market acceptance, respectively, and they determine recovered value, achievable target states, and restoration costs. We optimize the target state for each remanufacturing route, compare the routes, and then compare the optimized remanufacturing outcome with direct reuse and recycling. We analytically show that economically optimal remanufacturing need not fully restore a component to an as-new condition. The preferred target state may involve minimum restoration or full restoration, but also improvement mainly in one condition or intermediate improvement in both conditions. This choice depends on how the recovered value and restoration cost change with the extent of restoration, as well as the component's condition upon return, geometric complexity, and accessibility difficulty. Through a numerical study, we show that direct reuse, remanufacturing, and recycling can each be optimal for components returned in different conditions. Remanufacturing using conventional manufacturing may work best when geometrical complexity and accessibility difficulty are low, while remanufacturing using additive manufacturing becomes more attractive when these factors make the conventional route costly. Compared to fixed rules that preselect the recovery strategy (e.g. reusing components that meet minimum condition requirements and recycling the rest), the proposed model increases net profit by more than 25% on average. Compared to the common practice of fully restoring components using conventional manufacturing, our model yields on average over 11 times the net profit.

title: From Climate Finance to Climate Justice: A Municipal Accountability Framework for Nepal

detail.title: From Climate Finance to Climate Justice: A Municipal Accountability Framework for Nepal

detail.abstract:
Climate finance in Nepal is increasingly tracked through national budgetary and financial management systems, but important gaps remain in determining whether expenditure reaches the communities most vulnerable to climate risks. This paper proposes the Municipal Climate Finance Traceability Framework (MCFTF), a four-layer accountability framework designed to connect fund-flow tracking and climate-budget tagging with vulnerability-based targeting and beneficiary verification.

The framework introduces five diagnostic indicators: Public-to-Municipal Leverage Ratio (Lm), Concessional Capital Intensity (Ic), Vulnerability-Weighted Disbursement Ratio (VWDR), Distributional Lag Index (DLI), and Downward Accountability Completion Rate (DACR). It is designed to build on existing public financial management systems, particularly SuTRA and Climate Budget Tagging, rather than create parallel institutional structures.

A documentary feasibility review of Bheemdutta Municipality, using audited project financial statements and other available documents, examines the extent to which existing records can support the proposed framework. The review finds partial availability of financial information but significant gaps in ward-level expenditure, vulnerability data, and beneficiary verification.

The paper contributes a proposed accountability framework for examining the distributional dimension of municipal climate finance in Nepal. It does not claim institutional endorsement or empirical validation. Instead, it identifies data requirements, methodological limitations, and a phased pathway for technical review and pilot development.

title: Share Without Profit? Subsidies and the Money-To-Capability Step in Chinese Industrial Policy

detail.title: Share Without Profit? Subsidies and the Money-To-Capability Step in Chinese Industrial Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: China supplies 96 per cent of the EU's imported solar panels and 86 per cent of its imported batteries. We ask what the support behind that share left in the firms. We set customs data on EU imports for 2017-2025 beside economic-profit data on Chinese listed firms in nine sectors for 2015-2025. Unlike accounting profit or markups, economic profit charges each firm for the capital it uses. We find that China won three EU import markets as an industry while profit stayed with very few firms. Chinese solar makers earned 11.5 per cent of revenue above their cost of capital over 2015-22 and lost 3.1 per cent over 2023-25, while their share of EU imports held above 95 per cent. Half of that was a polysilicon price spike. In batteries and electric vehicles one firm in each sector, CATL and BYD, earns almost all the positive economic profit. CATL's rivals earn what an ordinary group of large Chinese firms earns, and neither leader disclosed more government grants per dollar of revenue than its rivals. In five of the eight sectors where US or EU makers are listed, they earned more than Chinese makers, though in solar the US maker's margin rests on its own tax credits. Trade and strategy theory predict this pattern when support is open to every firm: support buys entry, and entry competes profit away to buyers. Support that every rival can claim cannot be what a firm's profit rests on. For governments deciding whether to match or offset Chinese support, the question is less how much Beijing spent than what its money could not buy.

detail.abstract:
Data collection for this study began in 2020, when the world faced one of its greatest crises: the COVID-19 pandemic. In this context, the concept of “work” acquired new meanings, as did the relationship between employer and employee. The challenges were numerous, and many of their eﬀects remain apparent today.

Despite the changes brought about by the pandemic, the need to understand the factors underpinning professionals' decisions to remain with an organization remained constant. Reasons for the topic's continuing relevance include the high costs of replacing employees and retaining a dissatisfied workforce, demographic changes in the labor market, and the impact of the widespread circulation of information lacking scientific grounding, both in organizations and throughout professionals' careers.

Studies estimate that the costs of replacing professionals in operational and tactical positions range from 50% to 100% of their salary, also taking into account indirect costs associated with the process. For strategic positions, this figure can reach 200% of compensation. Moreover, retaining dissatisfied employees has consequences such as increased rework, reduced productivity and negative emotional eﬀects on colleagues (Climek, Henry & Jeong, 2024).

The challenge becomes even more complex given the labor market's current demographic composition, characterized by the retirement of experienced professionals, the entry of young people whose education was strongly aﬀected by the pandemic, and diﬀerent generations working together in the same professional environment.

In this context, generations have been widely discussed and, at times, treated superficially, with the spread of stereotypes and “absolute truths” lacking scientific rigor. Such generalizations are frequently used to inform organizational practices, even when they lack empirical grounding. Analysis of diﬀerent age groups was therefore included in this study, although it was not its sole focus.

This report's main objective is therefore to present, clearly and practically, knowledge derived from a reliable, scientifically grounded methodology. After three years of data collection, it was possible to analyze the pandemic period and the beginning of its post-crisis phase, incorporating phenomena such as the Great Resignation, the #quittingmyjob movement on TikTok and, more recently, Quiet Quitting. Today, the so-called “new normal” coexists with elements of the “old normal,” with many organizations gradually returning to on-site work.

detail.abstract: Since 2014 the world economy has absorbed a sequence of geopolitical shocks: sanctions, trade wars, a war in Europe, attacks on Red Sea shipping, sweeping tariffs and, in 2026, a war in the Gulf that cut oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz to a trickle. This policy report asks what the research evidence can tell policymakers about the consequences of such shocks. It draws on a systematic review of 3,570 peer-reviewed studies published between 1990 and 2026, combined with a detailed classification of a representative sample of 400 studies by source of geopolitical pressure, transmission channel, domain affected, who bears the consequences and how actors respond. The evidence is strongest for financial and energy markets, of medium strength for inflation, trade, supply chains and foreign investment, contested for the energy transition, and thin for food security, development and household welfare. Only 7% of studies test the channel through which shocks travel, households are the focus of just 6%, and reshoring and friend-shoring are evaluated in only 6 of the 355 studies coded in detail. The report identifies five blind spots that can mislead policy, rooted in the “riskification” of geopolitics: its reduction to a single news-based risk index. It sets out 22 recommendations for finance ministries, central banks, trade and energy authorities, economies of the Global South including the Middle East and North Africa, international organisations and research institutions, together with a three-phase implementation roadmap and indicators for monitoring progress. detail.abstract: People increasingly ask AI assistants whether an investment is safe before committing money. This study asks whether language models warn users about schemes that financial regulators have publicly flagged, and whether they do so as readily for schemes flagged by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Nigeria (SEC Nigeria) as for those on the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Warning List. Using an answer key drawn from regulatory records, with legitimate registered firms from both countries as controls, I asked two models, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Qwen3-8B, about 20 entities in English and Nigerian Pidgin, producing 80 answers. Only three of 40 answers about flagged schemes gave a warning based on knowledge of the scheme, all concerning the most prominent one, and no UK-flagged scheme received such a warning. Claude usually declined to recognise entities, whereas Qwen asserted facts, several apparently invented. Claude affirmed legitimate UK firms without qualification in five of ten answers, against one of ten for Nigerian firms. In Pidgin, Qwen read a flagged scheme's name as a reference to Nigeria itself and called it legitimate. These single-coder pilot findings are descriptive, but they point to gaps in entity recognition, factual reliability and language robustness.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a discrete-time framework for volatility modelling and derivative pricing based on polynomial preservation. The framework provides exact moments of arbitrary order and serial cross-moments of variance and return processes over any finite horizon through finite-dimensional matrix representations. This analytical tractability is maintained while accommodating flexible leverage and variance-of-variance dynamics and non-Gaussian innovations. We introduce two novel classes of stochastic volatility models that nest widely used discretetime specifications and study their statistical properties. Under two distinct scaling regimes, we establish weak convergence to polynomial diffusions and jump-diffusions and convergence of polynomial moments, linking discrete-time moment recursions to continuous-time matrixexponential formulas. An empirical analysis of S&P 500 returns and a large panel of options spanning 1996-2023 shows that the proposed specifications improve return fit and reduce mean weekly implied volatility root mean squared errors by approximately 8-41% relative to their nested benchmarks, depending on the variance dynamics and innovation distribution.

detail.abstract: We execute and evaluate an options margining methodology comprising a SABR stochastic-volatility fit to the implied volatility smile, the Barone-Adesi and Whaley (1987) quadratic approximation for American option prices, and a 99% historical-simulation Value-at-Risk (VaR) in which every scenario is fully revalued rather than approximated by a delta-gamma expansion. Although the framework was developed for options on interest rate futures, we apply it to SPY options using the general cost-of-carry formulation that the contracts' early-exercise feature requires. We run the pipeline on two independently sourced datasets, 2023-12-29 (OptionsDX) and 2026-06-01 (Databento OPRA, 353 sessions, acquired for 8.11), obtaining one-day 99% VaR of 2.4488 and 4.1216, or 36.89% and 28.58% of position value. Re-pricing the first date with the second vendor's data yields negligible differences in prices, implied volatilities and put-call-parity forwards, implying that the gap between the two cases reflects market conditions rather than data-feed effects. We identify two precision floors the methodology cannot escape: the quadratic approximation introduces roughly 1% error into every scenario P&L, amplified 5.5times relative to the price-level error because its sign changes with moneyness; and the ambiguity of ``linear interpolation'' in the specification changes VaR by 1.46% in the first case and 21.26% in the second. The dominant sensitivity, however, is the composition of the lookback window, which we demonstrate within a single continuous dataset by watching the April 2025 selloff age out of the window between March and June 2026.

detail.abstract: AI is remarkable at recognizing patterns-processing vast amounts of data quickly and with increasing sophistication-but it struggles when faced with truly novel situations, much like Kahneman's System 1 thinking. In contrast, the immune system operates more like System 2: refined over millions of years, it carefully distinguishes self from non-self, generates solutions to previously unseen threats, and maintains lifelong memory to fine-tune its responses. This Perspective paper suggests that AI and immune intelligence are not rivals but complement each other. Together, they can inspire not just better algorithms, but new ways for society to stay resilient, adaptable, and thoughtful in the face of rapid technological change.

detail.abstract: High-growth firms are disproportionately responsible for job creation and productivity gains in emerging economies, yet little is known about how the urban environments in which they operate shape their decisions to sell abroad and the returns they earn from doing so. Integrating real options reasoning with an institution-based view of urban task environments, we argue that city-level sentiment about economic development and technological disruption functions as a collective signal that shapes how high-growth firms value and exploit international opportunities. We combine a simulated firm-level survey dataset calibrated to the World Bank Enterprise Survey design for 25 Chinese cities (N = 2,700 firms; 540 high-growth firms) with city-industry sentiment scores produced through large language model text classification. Economic development sentiment is positively associated with export intensity, whereas technological disruption sentiment displays an inverted U-shaped relationship with export intensity. Exporting is associated with higher productivity and growth, but these returns are amplified by favorable development sentiment and attenuated by intense disruption sentiment. A multiverse analysis of 72 specifications supports the robustness of the core moderation result. The study advances research on emerging-market internationalization, high-growth entrepreneurship, and text-based measurement in international business.

title: Meta and Google are Wiring the World's Oceans: What does this Mean for Geopolitics and Business?

detail.title: Meta and Google are Wiring the World's Oceans: What does this Mean for Geopolitics and Business?

affiliations.org_name: HEC Paris (Groupe HEC) - Strategy & Business Policy

detail.abstract:
Submarine cables transmitting most intercontinental communications are a foundation
of the world’s economy. For policymakers, they are a strategic infrastructure that must be
secured in case of conflict and whose resilience must be improved. They are largely built
and operated by privately owned firms, yet policymakers rarely make explicit how these busi-
nesses make money and how this ultimately matters to the resilience of the cable network.
In this paper, I focus on the growing role taken in the submarine cable sector by so-called
Big Tech (or “hyperscaler”) firms—Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Meta. I argue that the
causes of Big Tech’s growing role are typically misunderstood. Conventional wisdom sees
these investments and direct ownership as a simple consequence of their share of data traffic.
However, I find that two firms, Google and Meta, have come to dominate investment in
submarine cables. The routes they choose differ sharply from those taken by traditional actors
in the sector. They are more likely to avoid maritime chokepoints and they effectively create
alternative worldwide cable loops.
I argue that Google and Meta behave differently because they can uniquely capture posi-
tive security externalities from the resilience of their networks that other firms cannot capture.
Their shared business model based on advertising puts a unique premium on the integrity of
their global networks. This explains their peculiar choice of routes and why other players do
not follow suit.
For policymakers, the first lesson is that Google and Meta have become suppliers of com-
munication resilience at a global scale. This alleviates concerns about resilience but, at the
same time, creates another set of dependencies. The second lesson is that policymakers must
understand in depth the internal logic of private actors, beyond what conventional wisdom
may suggest, to anticipate their incentives, decisions and the geopolitical implications.

detail.abstract: Policies involving what are known as Free Economic Zones (FEZs) have been popular among countries interested in attracting foreign investment. While foreign investment has generally benefited the receiving country, the effect of market rivalry is known to reverse this impact. Our paper tests, using listed and unlisted companies in Korea, whether the designation of a Korean FEZ affects firms in the region positively in terms of sales, profit, productivity, and export activities. We find that FEZ-designated firms outperform those in the other regions. However, the findings also suggest that the impact of FEZ designation takes years to unfold and that success requires consistent effort.

detail.abstract: Many previous studies conclude that population aging leads to an increase in consumption or income inequality. The results are based on a conventional model that analyzes compositional effects given interage differences in the means and variances of income. These issues are addressed in this paper by (1) developing a new empirical strategy for estimating the effects of population aging, income, and other socio-economic variables on living arrangements; (2) extending the standard model of income inequality to incorporate responses in relation to one aspect of the familial support system – the formation of multi-generational households (or extended households); and (3) applying the models to South Korea, where familial support has been important source of consumption for older people. In particular, this paper complements previous studies by incorporating the responses of familial support systems to changes in the age distribution of the population. Our model and empirical results suggest that (1) population aging could have led to a greater increase in the proportion living in extended households, but improvements in survival have had a weaker effect than the fertility decline on the proportion of people living in extended households, (2) higher incomes of workers in Korea could have led to more of a shift away from extended households, and (3) an increase in both the proportion of the family cohort and the proportion of pensioners living in extended households reduces the variance in income. These results support the argument that co-residence and population aging may reduce income inequality.

detail.abstract: This study investigates whether Saitdol loans, a type of government-guaranteed loan, were allocated to groups that would otherwise be unable to access the loan market without such a guarantee. To assess this, both non-parametric and parametric estimation methods, as proposed by Hendren (2013), were employed to examine the severity of information asymmetry between Saitdol loan borrowers and financial institutions, a potential cause of a market failure. The analysis results indicate that the information asymmetry between borrowers holding Saitdol loans and financial institutions was not severe enough to cause a market failure. This suggests that a significant number of Saitdol loans were allocated to borrowers who could have obtained loans from the private sector without government guarantees.

detail.abstract: Procedural law has refined, over half a century, the individual's right to be heard before an institution acts against her. Yet the suffering that institutions produce through ordinary operation, such as exhausted staff, unanswered petitioners and complaints that accumulate without ever becoming cases, rarely reaches any hearing, because no decision is pending when it is first signalled. This article asks whether the principal hearing doctrines of the United States, England and Wales, Germany and the European Union, and Brazil are structurally incapable of reaching that upstream layer, and what law could do about it without reproducing the problem it addresses. The method is doctrinal and comparative, supplemented by an interpretive reading of Oliveira's novel O Prédio que Aprendeu a Escutar, treated as an analytical case and not as evidence. The article advances a doctrinal and interpretive thesis: the hearing instruments examined are decision-indexed, that is, triggered by an anticipated adverse measure against an identified person, while the instruments that operate outside decisions (general good-administration standards, Brazilian service-user legislation, ombudsman principles, psychosocial risk regulation) convert human signals into administrative data without attaching a duty to answer. The contribution is a distinction among hearing, listening and response, and a modest interpretive proposal: a duty to record and answer with reasons when documented, repeated signals indicate a risk to identifiable persons, designed to resist ritual compliance. The thesis is tested against three objections, including the objection that proceduralized listening is itself a form of indifference, and its limits are stated.

detail.abstract: Occupational licensing is meant to protect consumers, but it also raises the cost of entering a profession. Cosmetology is a useful test case: in 2017 states required anywhere from 1,000 to 2,300 hours of training for the same license. I combine these requirements with Census Bureau counts of beauty salons, including businesses with no employees, in two ways. Across states in 2017, 100 more required hours is associated with 0.52 fewer salons per 10,000 residents, about 2 percent of the average (p = 0.06). That association comes mostly from differences between regions: it disappears when states are compared only with others in their own Census region or when Southern states are excluded. I then follow Idaho, Nebraska, and South Dakota, which cut their requirements by 300 to 600 hours in 2018, using a difference-indifferences design with 33 states whose rules did not change. Salon density in the reform states rose 3.7 percent relative to the comparison states, but placebo tests show that changes this large are common by chance (p = 0.52), and pre-reform trends were similar. Neither design finds clear evidence that training requirements reduce the number of salons, though both are too imprecise to rule out effects of the size the cross-section suggests.

detail.abstract: Seismic codes and standards still rest on equivalent loads, reduction factors, and a long list of supplementary provisions. These tools were created when nonlinear time history analysis was too slow and too complex for everyday design. That limit no longer exists, but the design philosophy built on it has not changed. This article presents the collapse-based design (CBD) method philosophy, an independent framework for the seismic analysis, design, evaluation, and retrofitting of structures. The method rests on two principles: the structure is analyzed under the seismic intensity at which it is expected to collapse, and every member is designed for its maximum capacity under the loads produced at that intensity. The collapse intensity is found before the analysis with the collapse spectrum, which raises the design spectrum with three scale factors: the spectral acceleration ratio, the design spectrum ratio, and the collapse margin ratio. The analysis is an incremental nonlinear time history analysis performed quickly with the endurance time method. Ductile members are designed for their ultimate plastic capacity, non-ductile members for their ultimate elastic capacity, and connections and foundations for the maximum loads transferred to them. Because the analysis reaches the ultimate capacity, the effects of overstrength, ductility, irregularity, P-delta, and other modeled factors enter the results directly, and the response modification factor, overstrength factor, deflection amplification factor, target displacement, performance levels, capacity design, and strong column-weak beam checks are not needed. The same analysis also gives the collapse margin ratio, a dynamic capacity curve, and the behavior at every hazard level. The article explains the philosophy, theory, equations, step-by-step procedure, design notes, comparison with existing methods, results of the studies published so far, advantages and limitations, and the potential of CBD as a unifying framework for earthquake engineering practices.

detail.abstract: Machine learning can identify suspicious cloud activity at volumes that exceed manual review capacity. Its operational value depends on how well a detection policy handles rare incidents, incomplete audit evidence and differences in the consequences of compromise. This study combines a targeted synthesis of intrusion detection, model calibration and cloud audit research with a deterministic sensitivity analysis at the candidate-case level. Four models quantify alert precision under changing incident prevalence, review demand under a finite analyst budget, the conditions under which a high-impact case should outrank a higher-probability case, and the effects of unequal evidence coverage on incident recovery. In a worked scenario of 100,000 candidate cases, 0.05% incident prevalence and 80% recall, a 0.1% false-positive rate produces about 140 alerts and 28.6% precision. A capacity of 100 reviews limits the feasible false-positive rate to approximately 0.0600% at the same recall. When incident observability falls from 90% to 50%, end-to-end recall falls from 72% to 40% with conditional recall fixed at 80%. These results arise from stated assumptions and can be reproduced directly from the equations. They motivate an evaluation protocol that joins chronological and account-held-out tests with evidence coverage, analyst workload and calibration checks. The study identifies which quantities a cloud security team must estimate before using machine learning scores to allocate response capacity. AI disclosure. OpenAI Codex assisted with drafting, source discovery, analytical calculations and figure preparation.

detail.abstract: Purpose. This paper specifies Systemic Strategy-to-Implementation Orchestration (SSIO), a governance protocol for connecting demand generation, qualification, selling, operational commitment, delivery, invoicing, and collected cash in B2B industrial enterprises. It addresses a recurring design failure: commercial functions optimize local activity while the enterprise lacks a verifiable end-to-end account of value conversion. Design/methodology/approach. SSIO is presented as a conceptual, design-oriented management protocol synthesized from systems thinking, feedback control, customer relationship management, strategy execution, and operations management. It translates these foundations into five waste vortexes, a contrast architecture, four deployment phases, governance routines, and measurable propositions. The framework is not presented as a tested causal model; implementation evidence and outcome estimates require organization-specific validation. Findings. The protocol treats revenue as a cross-functional flow rather than a sales-department output. Its central mechanism is a closed loop in which outcome data—especially delivery performance, margin, cash collection, and loss reasons—changes upstream targeting, qualification, promises, and capacity allocation. Explicit stage evidence, data stewardship, service-level agreements, and capacity gates reduce ambiguity at handoffs and make constraints visible. Practical implications. Executives can use SSIO to map lead-to-cash, define common data and stage semantics, establish accountable ownership, align sales commitments with feasible delivery, and review leading and lagging indicators in a revenue command cadence. Technology is an enabling substrate, not a substitute for process ownership or decision rights. Originality/value. SSIO integrates commercial pipeline governance with delivery-capacity and cashrealization controls. Its contribution is a testable architecture for preventing the automation of disconnected processes and for extending revenue operations beyond opportunity closure.

detail.abstract: We study how platform competition changes the welfare ranking of differential privacy standards. In a two-stage duopoly, platforms choose auditable privacy budgets before competing in user prices. Larger budgets improve data usability and monetization but weaken privacy protection. When they also reduce governance costs incurred at the platform level, symmetric equilibrium budgets exceed the symmetric welfare benchmark. For platforms differing only in query sensitivity, we compare a common privacy budget cap with a common accuracy cap, optimizing each rule's level. For general technology functions, our baseline welfare analysis shows that the accuracy cap's second-order advantage declines as price rivalry weakens. This local ranking around symmetry can reverse at most once, toward the common budget cap. Competition affects the welfare consequences of reallocating consumers across platforms, so equalizing accuracy need not provide the appropriate sensitivity adjustment. In particular, the accuracy rule can adjust budgets too much even when the direction of adjustment is desirable. A rule matching the welfare benchmark's first-order sensitivity response eliminates the second-order welfare loss. The local gross welfare gain from differentiated caps vanishes as platforms become alike, so any fixed additional implementation cost favors uniform caps sufficiently close to symmetry.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation in higher education is fundamentally changing management and training approaches. However, this process poses significant challenges in ensuring digital ethics and safety. This study analyzes the current situation and proposes solutions for addressing ethical and safety issues in digital transformation activities at Vietnamese higher education institutions. Through a multimethod research approach, integrating document analysis and field observation with empirical insights, the study identifies three main challenges: (1) limitations in infrastructure and technology, (2) gaps in digital capabilities, and (3) lack of an integrated management framework. Based on these findings, the study proposes an integrated and process-oriented management framework named CoMDES, encompassing policy, technology, and human resource development solutions whose applicability is illustrated in a specific institutional context. The research findings enhance the theoretical foundation for addressing digital ethics and safety issues in educational contexts while offering practical recommendations for educational managers amid widespread digital transformation.

detail.abstract: Advances in autonomous driving are shifting mobility services from vehicle intelligence to fleet intelligence, necessitating centralized and anticipatory fleet control. This requires large-scale, interdependent decisions that account for stochastic demand and its downstream effects on fleet availability. This paper models dynamic ridesharing as a period-based Markov decision process (MDP), enabling fleetwide reoptimization of request commitment, pooling, routing and repositioning. First, we formulate a subpath-based set-partitioning model over a time-space network, embedding high-dimensional value information through subpath synergies, yielding a quadratically constrained quadratic program with binary variables (QCQP-B). Second, we develop an exact, scalable column-and-row generation algorithm for canonical QCQP-B, establishing convergence criteria for column-dependent row structures. Third, motivated by integer-induced value discontinuities across resource states, we develop an optimize-to-learn algorithm that leverages structural priors from integer optimization within a model tree, improving the bias–variance tradeoff in value learning. Experiments on real-world data show that our optimization algorithm improves solution efficiency by 63–80% over the state-of-the-art approach, while our learning algorithm achieves 19–22% higher performance than myopic policy and 3–6% over the strongest benchmark. Compared with event-based and decoupled approaches, our period-based integrated reoptimization better balances anticipatory information, fleetwide coordination and execution efficiency, facilitating efficient, reliable and scalable mobility services.

detail.abstract: Securing air and space defense superiority against resource-heavy competitors through symmetrical hardware matching is financially unsustainable for fiscally constrained rising powers like India. This study introduces The Chanakyan Gambit, an interdisciplinary strategic architecture synthesizing Kautilya’s Saptanga theory of statecraft, Ricardian Comparative Advantage, and behavioral game theory to generate asymmetric cost-imposing capabilities. By operationalizing indigenous defense software engineering, artificial intelligence, and network-centric interoperability through a Fast-Track Digital Procurement Sandbox (FT-DPS), the model resolves bureaucratic risk aversion and vendor adverse selection using legal safe harbors and milestone-gated contracts. Furthermore, incorporating Quantal Response Equilibria, Prospect Theory, and Bayesian trust updates neutralizes technology hold-up risks and endogenously builds structural trust within international defense partnerships. Validated across 50 Indian defense technology cases and 20 international partnership tracks, this framework provides a predictive, mathematically grounded 10-year roadmap for modern defense procurement and regional deterrence

detail.abstract: Senegalese public universities, such as Gaston Berger University (GBU) in Saint-Louis, face recurring crises that undermine their operations and reputation. These crises are defined as destabilizing processes. They include strikes, demands for changes to study conditions, perceived insufficient funding, and governance widely seen as failing. Using processual and event-based approaches to crisis, we analyze how actors at GBU neglect values in their management practices. We used a qualitative approach and conducted 26 semi-structured interviews with teachers, administrative staff, and students. Our results reveal two types of crises: the first, called processual, includes internal conflicts, reforms, and massification; the second, called event-based, includes the COVID-19 crisis and the political crises of 2022-2024. These findings highlight the intertwining and persistence of crises, exacerbated by neglected organizational values, with detrimental administrative and organizational consequences, such as the invalidation of academic years, contested political decisions, and a lack of collaboration among actors.
