keywords: Organizational Effectiveness and Value Creation outcome measurement

detail.abstract: Organizations often measure what is easy to count rather than what creates value. Hours logged, tickets closed, tasks completed, features shipped and AI tools deployed describe activity, but they do not necessarily show whether customers, employees or the business are better off. Artificial intelligence increases the importance of this distinction because it can multiply output without guaranteeing improved quality, decision-making or business results. This paper examines the proposition that organizations in the AI age should measure outcomes rather than activity alone. It develops a three-layer perspective covering customer and value outcomes, flow, and organizational capability. The paper draws on selected literature and published organizational examples, including DBS Bank's Managing Through Journeys approach and the Wells Fargo cross-selling scandal. It proposes practical measurement principles that pair speed and volume indicators with quality, rework and customer impact; limit the number of outcome measures; assign metric ownership; and review measures that no longer support sound decisions. The paper is conceptual and relies on secondary sources. It does not present primary empirical findings or claim to establish causal relationships. Its contribution is a practical measurement perspective for distinguishing activity from progress and for assessing whether AI-enabled work produces sustained value.

detail.abstract: Authorisation to use an autonomous weapon depends on people, information and powers that can change after approval. This article proposes an international duty to maintain an assessable account of those supervisory conditions and use changes in that account when deciding whether autonomous functions may continue. Its purpose is civilian protection and responsibility that remains attributable through technological and organisational change. Doctrinal analysis connects the proposal to weapons review, precautions, legal advice and command duties. Comparison with human control, national re-review and safety assurance identifies substantial existing resources. Public material on Patriot documents mismatches between supervisory assumptions and actual capacity; it leaves the prevalence of an unassigned legal decision path unresolved. That distinction limits the case for additional international regulation. Second-order cybernetics supplies a functional criterion: an institution represents a change in its own capacity to assess and correct action, and uses that representation in further regulation. Material Change Authorisation (MCA) translates this criterion into proposed duties concerning records, decisions, interim protection and independent review. Model provisions also address prohibited capabilities, preventive controls and international implementation reporting. Fictional organisational examples illustrate the evidential distinction. A prospective protocol compares the mechanism with competent existing practice and a matched structured checklist, using independently prepared legal benchmarks. The contribution is a testable legal design; its comparative protective effectiveness and the necessity of a new international obligation remain questions for implementation research.

detail.abstract: Problem Definition: We investigate how affiliation with Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) affects skilled nursing facilities' (SNFs) financial performance and how ACOs can design sustainable postacute-care networks. Academic/Practical Relevance: Although ACOs and integrated care systems promote coordination across healthcare providers, the financial benefits of integration may not extend to individual participating organizations. Understanding these consequences is important for sustaining integrated healthcare delivery. Methodology: We analyze a national panel of U.S. SNFs from 2020 to 2023 using an instrumental variable approach. We further develop a two-stage stochastic optimization model that incorporates empirically informed SNF participation requirements into ACO network and contract design. Results: ACO affiliation significantly increases net patient revenue and operating expenses without significantly improving net income. These findings persist with longer ACO exposure. Mechanism analyses indicate that affiliation increases Medicare postacute activity without significantly increasing overall patient throughput, accompanied by higher salary and overhead expenses. These increased costs are not accompanied by significant improvements in care-transition quality outcomes. Our modeling results show that optimal network design is sensitive to patient demand, SNF participation requirements, and the ACO's share of spending reductions. Importantly, contracting with additional SNFs is not always financially beneficial. Managerial Implications: Our findings highlight the potential misalignment between system-level benefits and individual providers' financial incentives. Sustainable ACO networks require balancing potential spending reductions against the compensation needed to secure SNF participation.

detail.abstract: Studies dispute whether bond purchases lower yields through their size or through the signal of central bank presence. Announcements usually state amounts and cannot separate the two, but China's bond trading facility announced entry and exit without amounts. Using fifteen-minute Treasury futures, we find that all three announcements ranked within the most extreme 8.35 per cent of trading days. Amount releases moved futures no more than ordinary days, although monthly amounts varied fifteen-fold. This first high-frequency evaluation of the facility indicates that investors price presence more than purchase size, so calibrating purchases to a yield target may be misplaced.

detail.abstract: We analyse the pricing of cross-border transfers by banks as well as money transfer operators (MTOs) when direct links connect national payment systems. Comparing remittance price quotes across the staggered activation of these links, we find that banks lower total fees at activation. However, this reduction does not extend to MTOs; their transfer fees rise at activation and their total fees are higher after one year, while bank fees remain lower. Both provider types initially lower FX margins. These results show that payment links lower banks' prices and suggest that providers with other settlement models do not share the benefit.

detail.abstract: We examine how a marketplace prices AI demand forecasts when competing sellers decide whether to subscribe before setting prices. Unlike independent providers, marketplaces also earn transaction commissions, creating an additional incentive to influence AI adoption. Consequently, marketplaces charge lower fees and expand access when additional subscriptions increase commission revenue, but the opposite occurs when this effect is negative. Beyond adoption, AI forecasts reshape competition by potentially disadvantaging uninformed rivals and reducing aggregate seller profits. Numerical analysis informed by Xianyu records further shows that broader AI adoption does not necessarily improve market outcomes, as consumer surplus and total welfare may decline.

detail.abstract: With four decades of Wall Street Journal articles, I identify the news on days when stocks and Treasuries fall together and separate news about interest rates from news about fiscal risk. My approach compares these broken hedge days with flight-to-quality days, when stocks fall just as sharply but Treasuries rally, and tests the reported news against data that journalists could not shape and against shocks identified from prices. I find that broken hedge days are days of news about interest rates, in every regime since 1984. Articles cite U.S. inflation and the Fed 15.5 percentage points more often on these days than on flight-to-quality days. In contrast, fiscal news does not distinguish the two types of day, and Treasury auctions and refunding announcements show no association with hedge failures. Most hedge failures occur on days without a scheduled announcement. On these days, rate news still distinguishes broken hedge days, and Fed communication between meetings is one of its sources. The broken hedge days of 2025 are an exception, since most of them show the price pattern of rising risk premia on U.S. assets rather than that of rate news.

detail.abstract: We use trademark registrations to identify green product activity in firms' core businesses and examine whether equity markets fully incorporate its value implications. Firms with such activity exhibit stronger subsequent operating performance and earn positive risk-adjusted returns, while analysts underestimate their future earnings. Green product activity predicts future stock returns after controlling for overall trademark intensity, green patent activity, standard return predictors, and industry effects. Abnormal returns are concentrated in the first post-formation year and in earnings-announcement months. Return predictability is stronger among firms with weaker environmental profiles, greater regulatory exposure, and greater valuation difficulty, as well as during periods of lower environmental salience. Overall, our findings are consistent with the gradual incorporation of value-relevant information about green product commercialization into stock prices, with stronger underreaction among firms with weaker environmental profiles and when the economic implications of green product activity are more difficult to assess.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of government venture capital (GVC) in addressing persistent gaps in Europe's risk capital. Unlike the US, Europe faces fragmented financial markets, lower risk tolerance and low levels of private institutional investment. National and EU-level GVC programmes can support high-potential firms, crowd in private investment and promote entrepreneurship. Drawing on recent data and case studies, the paper analyses the rationale for public intervention, typologies of GVC models, design features and interactions with other policy tools. It also provides policy recommendations to enhance the effectiveness, strategic alignment, and governance of GVC programmes in Europe within broader industrial policy frameworks.

detail.abstract: Short-time work (STW) schemes were widely deployed during COVID-19 to stabilize employment, while the same crisis also accelerated firm digitalization, potentially reshaping firm-level labor demand. We examine how these responses relate to firms' employment and productivity trajectories during and beyond the shock. Using the German Innovation Survey (2012-2024) and a dynamic difference-indifferences approach, we find that STW is associated with lower employment through 2024, alongside a productivity recovery from 2022 onward. Firms with STW shrank relative to comparable firms that did not use the scheme and became, at most, slightly leaner. Digitalization in response to the crisis is associated with sustained employment growth, but this advantage weakens with STW intensity and is not matched by productivity gains. We highlight a tension between protecting existing jobs and adapting to a crisis that rewarded changes in how firms operate.

detail.abstract: Previous work shows that when firms choose the direction of their research before how much to invest, a generous patent regime can induce them to inefficiently converge on the same technological area. We ask whether technology licensing, via fixed fees or per-unit royalties, corrects this failure. The answer rests on cross-licensing: under both contracts, the prospect of combining complementary innovations developed along different trajectories can lead firms to differentiate. In a Cournot illustration, the inefficiency survives only when innovations are close substitutes and products are not too differentiated: then the cross-license adds little to what each firm already owns or, when one firm invests more, research along different trajectories becomes a contest to supply the technology both firms use. In the same illustration, lump-sum fees dominate per-unit royalties in terms of welfare. Technology markets and patentability requirements thus appear to be complementary instruments, and antitrust scrutiny should target the terms of cross-licensing agreements rather than the institution itself.

detail.abstract: More countries have made carbon neutral or net zero emission commitments since 2019. Within this context, reexamining the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) hypothesis plays an essential role in sizing up the global economic development situation and realizing the global carbon emission reduction target. A methodological challenge in testing the EKC hypothesis, which states that increasing income makes CO 2 emissions begin to decline beyond a turning point, lies in determining if this benchmark point exists. The EKC hypothesis between income and CO 2 emissions is reassessed by applying a new kink regression model for the G7 countries from 1890 to 2015. Results reveal the inverted U-shaped nexus does not exist for US, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan. For these five countries, the EKC curve has a turning point, but the positive impact of incomes on CO 2 emissions becomes significantly smaller after the turning point. We describe this relationship as a pseudo-EKC. K.U.K. and France are the only exceptions, fitting the EKC hypothesis. Further analysis indicates that the relationship between income and SO 2 emissions presents an inverted U-shaped curve. Moreover, we observe that the turning point occurs at different points in time for the different G7 countries. Therefore, environmental policies targeting pollutant emission reduction should consider the different characteristics of different pollutants and regions. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.3390/su14073955

detail.abstract:
We test whether a correlated random-level (CRL) volatility model with one-dimensional quadrature pricing fits and hedges S&P 500 options better than SSVI and Heston, using 168 month-ends from 2010 to 2023 and daily data for 2020 and 2022. CRL and SSVI fit equally well (median implied-volatility RMSE 0.38 and 0.39 points; Heston 0.51), CRL at the short end and in the put wing, SSVI at the long end and in the call wing. A correlation that falls with maturity lowers the median error to 0.28 points and beats constant correlation out of sample on 95% of dates, by only 5.5%. The local volatility of the fitted surfaces is in closed form and positive on every date. The fit does not carry over to hedging: frozen-parameter CRL, SSVI and Heston deltas lose to Black-Scholes, and a delta that learns the level from returns loses to the Hull-White minimum-variance delta.
The model is introduced in Islyaev (2026), "A Correlated Random-Level Volatility Model: Exact One-Dimensional Pricing with Skew", https://ssrn.com/abstract=7664360.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the alternating-move duopoly model of Maskin and Tirole (1988b) through a laboratory experiment. Four treatments vary market conditions for the first time in the literature: the continuation probability of games, the exogenous initial market price, and the firms' production capacity constraints. This is a relatively less complex strategy than the two rather complex equilibria described in Maskin-Tirole.

detail.abstract: Market makers and HFT firms face adverse selection when trading against informed order flow. This phenomenon, known as order flow toxicity, erodes profitability and increases risk. While theoretical models exist, practical detection of toxicity in real-time remains challenging, especially in cryptocurrency markets. We build and validate a machine learning detector that predicts whether a given trade will be toxic (i.e., price moves against the aggressor within a 500ms horizon) using L2 order book and trade flow features. We use 1.6 million aggregated trades and bookTicker updates for BTCUSDT perpetual futures on Binance for January 2, 2024. We compute four microstructure features: Order Flow Imbalance (OFI), Microprice Deviation, Queue Imbalance, and a VPIN-like proxy. A LightGBM classifier is trained on the first 80% of the day and tested on the last 20% (time-based split). The detector achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.66 (Deflated AUC > 0.95, indicating statistical significance). Filtering out trades with predicted toxicity > 0.6 removes 12.9% of trades and reduces the toxicity rate from 13.08% to 10.48%. Our work demonstrates that toxicity is predictable using publicly available L2 data. The proposed detector can be integrated into marketmaking systems to reduce adverse selection without requiring proprietary data.

detail.abstract: The free flow of energy cannot be fully achieved in China's energy market because of incomplete market-oriented reform, resulting in energy allocation distortion, which has hampered carbon emissions reduction. However, the extent of energy allocation distortion and its role in carbon emission efficiency remain unexplored. Therefore, this study aims to measure energy allocation distortion and investigate its impact on carbon emission efficiency. For this purpose, first, we derive energy allocation distortion based on a production function and carbon emission efficiency using a meta-frontier non-radial Malmquist index. To effectively address the endogeneity issue, we use a generalized method of moments model to estimate the impact of energy allocation distortion on carbon emission efficiency. Second, we further explore the distortionary mechanism of carbon emission efficiency associated with energy allocation and analyze the asymmetric effect of energy allocation distortion on carbon emission efficiency. The results show a certain degree of energy allocation distortion throughout the country, and disparity exists among different regions. The average value of carbon emission efficiency in the eastern region is 1.0286, well ahead of the national average, demonstrating better performance than other regions. Energy allocation distortion negatively affects carbon emission efficiency, with a 1% increase in energy allocation distortion leading to a 0.251% decrease in carbon emission efficiency. Technological progress, the structure of energy consumption, and industrial structure are important transmission channels through which energy allocation affects carbon emission efficiency. The study contributes to uncovering regional energy allocation distortion and its impacts on carbon emission efficiency and providing strategic policy recommendations for improving energy allocation efficiency. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.118241

detail.abstract: We study approximations of a basket or spread S = ∑︁ i wiFi of n correlated SABR forwards by a one-factor displaced SABR model. An exact pathwise volatility decomposition identifies the covariance and drift terms that the target approximates. The Kienitz-Wittke (2010) parameter formulas agree with a frozen-weight, first-order Gaussian-regression construction, defined here as FRZ. Under smoothness, nondegeneracy and localisation hypotheses we derive the short-strike jet of the Riemannian distance to the strike hypersurface in the metric g = a-1 and relate it to the leading normal implied-volatility smile. For normal SABR baskets we identify the small-time conditional local variance with the basket variance at the closest point; for absorbed CEV baskets we establish a strip-conditioned leading limit. Under explicit density and tail assumptions we derive the first-order relation between time-dependent local volatility and normal implied volatility, its inversion, and its consistency with a constrained Laplace expansion. The effective basket SABR of Hagan, Lesniewski, Skoufis and Woodward is expressed in the same invariants. We compare several projection and calibration methods on stated examples and random parameter samples, using conditional Monte Carlo, Monte Carlo and PDE pricing. The comparisons include sampling and discretisation error and are not uniform accuracy guarantees. Moment-based and displaced-target constructions require separate moment, support and martingale admissibility checks, which we state. For normal factors the characteristic function of the basket is reduced exactly to one parabolic equation in the volatility variables, which gives the basket smile at all maturities without simulation; the law at T = ∞ exists and is Cauchy under an isotropy condition on the correlations, which for two factors is also necessary.

detail.abstract: This article asks whether open banking has transformed retail banking and, if not, where the mechanism that was expected to produce the change fails. It compares regimes in which data access is mandated by law (the EU/EEA and the United Kingdom under the revised Payment Services Directive, PSD2) with market-led data sharing in the United States. A narrative review is combined with descriptive analyses of World Bank Global Findex, IMF, Crunchbase, and Eurostat data, an evidence table of 127 obstacle reports from 81 sources, and process tracing of four cases. Account ownership in Europe rose from 90.6% in 2017 to 95.5% in 2021, but the rise was concentrated in six economies with low initial ownership; branch density fell at the same annual rate before and after PSD2 (about 5%); and FinTech formation in 20182021 grew at a similar pace in four European countries (77%) and in the United States (85%). Regulatory-led regimes report problems with the quality, cost, and enforcement of mandated access; market-led regimes report the lack of an enforceable right, screen scraping, and concentrated data aggregators; low consumer trust is reported under both models. A legal mandate secures an enforceable and regulated right of access, but it is neither necessary for data sharing at scale nor sucient for adoption: with a mandate the mechanism stalls at services and stalls or breaks at consumer use, and without one it breaks at the access right itself.

detail.abstract: Why does informal financing remain prevalent in emerging markets? We propose a mobility-aspiration framework linking perceived upward mobility shaped by meritocratic institutions to corporate financing through managerial aspirations for personal achievement. Using historical data from imperial China and LLM-analyzed modern corporate texts, we build a novel data set of upward mobility perceptions. Firms exposed to greater perceived upward mobility provide more unexpected trade credit to customers, particularly when managerial power allocation is unbalanced and empire-building incentives are stronger. These firms portray supply chain relationships as enduring and concentrated among fewer customers. However, modern anti-corruption institutions attenuate this unintended consequence.

detail.abstract:
Experts hold divergent views on AI and its potential impact on the labor market. Generative AI has the potential to improve workforce productivity by automating tasks, accelerating them, or reducing the skills required to perform them. As is true with any transformative technological change, there will be winners and losers. For example, automated telephone switching displaced switchboard operators but created new technical jobs in telecommunications maintenance and network management.

The rate at which AI diffuses through an economy and the effects it has on a labor market depend on factors such as industry composition, incumbent workers' skills, and the degree to which a nation’s infrastructure supports the many technical requirements of AI deployment. Despite the technological frontier being pushed forward almost exclusively in the United States and China, Israel and Singapore have seen the greatest level of AI utilization per capita. This suggests that AI innovators are not necessarily located in labor markets most ready to deploy and use generative solutions. This report outlines a framework for describing occupations in the context of AI, discusses labor conditions for large-scale AI adoption, proposes mitigation strategies that governments might implement to protect disaffected workers, and poses a series of open research questions that may be valuable to industry leaders and policymakers.

title: Does a Transparent Cross-Asset Regime Oscillator Time the S&P 500? A Pre-Registered Test of a Public TradingView Indicator

detail.title: Does a Transparent Cross-Asset Regime Oscillator Time the S&P 500? A Pre-Registered Test of a Public TradingView Indicator
detail.abstract: We test whether a simple, fully public market-regime gauge carries information about forward S&P 500 returns and whether a mechanical allocation rule built on it beats passive benchmarks after costs. The gauge is the open-source Cross-Asset Regime Oscillator published on TradingView: five daily cross-asset signals (high-yield versus Treasury ETF ratio, VIX, industrials versus utilities ETF ratio, the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury slope, and the ICE dollar index), each z-scored over 252 trading days, clamped, averaged with equal weight and mapped to a 0 to 100 score with five bands. We rebuild it from free data, pre-register hypotheses, horizons, statistics and one allocation rule before computing any forward return, verify the rebuild against the chart, and evaluate 2008 to 2026 with a chronological out-of-sample split, stationary block-bootstrap intervals and a reduced-signal check back to 1991. A rule holding 100/75/50/25/0 percent equity by band cuts the maximum drawdown from 52% to 20% at a risk-adjusted return not distinguishable from buy and hold or from a constant mix with the same average exposure (Sharpe 0.69 against 0.59, 90% interval on the gap -0.11 to +0.26). About two thirds of the drawdown reduction is the exposure removed; the rest, and the whole Sharpe gap, come from two crisis episodes and reverse before 2008. Forward returns by band form a U, not a ladder. The oscillator describes conditions and reduces drawdown; a timing edge beyond exposure is not established.

title: The algorithmic factory of young debtors: digital architecture, emotions and over-indebtedness in the fintech era

detail.title: The algorithmic factory of young debtors: digital architecture, emotions and over-indebtedness in the fintech era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Contemporary over-indebtedness is no longer driven exclusively by financial imbalances or errors in the rational assessment of individual risk. This paper argues that a significant share of emerging forms of insolvency constitutes an emotionally and technologically conditioned phenomenon that exceeds traditional approaches centered on financial literacy. Drawing on the intersection of bankruptcy law, behavioral economics, and cognitive sciences, it examines how fintech platforms and digital consumption architectures shape economic decisionmaking through the systematic exploitation of cognitive biases, heuristics, and states of emotional vulnerability, particularly among young people. From this perspective, the study analyzes the shift from the homo economicus paradigm to that of homo digitalis and develops the notion of the "heuristic debtor": a subject whose agency and decisional autonomy are not merely conditioned, but actively extracted by digital designs engineered to eliminate cognitive friction, accelerate consumption, and capitalize on phenomena such as doom spending, financial anxiety, and the fear of missing out (FOMO).

keywords: and the Difference Between Eligibility and Dependence Taiwan

detail.abstract: Proposals to extend Taiwan's silicon shield from semiconductor fabrication into the verification of trusted computing infrastructure meet a legal question before a technical one. A trust regime runs on recognition: relying parties must accept, under their own law, results that someone else produced. Most governments do not recognize Taiwan as a state, and the principal arrangement for mutual acceptance of information-technology security certificates admits only government agencies representing countries. This Article shows that the obstacle is narrower than it appears. Taiwan already participates in rule-bound regimes through capacities defined by function rather than status: as a separate customs territory in the World Trade Organization and a party to the Agreement on Government Procurement, as a fishing entity in regional fisheries management, through agreements concluded by the American Institute in Taiwan and given domestic effect by the Taiwan Relations Act, and through an accreditation body that has been a signatory to the international laboratory accreditation arrangement since 2000. Conformity assessment is the most developed of these channels because it asks about competence rather than sovereignty. The same feature sets its limit. A route that admits bodies by attributes others can acquire secures eligibility, the standing of a Taiwanese body's results to count, without securing dependence, a partner's continued need for them. A Taiwanese laboratory could keep every recognition it holds and lose its customers to another accredited laboratory without any government acting. Legal reliance written into a partner's procurement rules can make exclusion reasoned and reviewable; it cannot prevent substitution. Continued importance depends on access to manufacturing evidence and independence in assessing it, and that access thins as fabrication and packaging move abroad. Stated generally, certification confers network power only when accepted evidence is non-fungible: necessary to the relying party and difficult to reproduce elsewhere. The Article proposes a design that protects eligibility through accreditation, a narrow procurement pilot, a withdrawal procedure with expiring emergency suspension, and continuity arrangements that preserve past evidence without transferring signing authority, and it states what that design cannot do.

detail.abstract: This working paper examines how pre-market intraday microstructure and dynamic historical-analog weighting can help organize conditional short-horizon scenarios in 3× leveraged semiconductor ETFs. Extending FHAT Technical Note 068, we examine a failed overnight retest of the prior regular-session high, an interruption in the sequence of rising swing highs and lows, and a break below the five-minute MA500. A subsequent pre-market rebound stalled near 66.20. SOXL then fell below pre-market VWAP and the daily pivot (64.57), increasing the qualitative weight assigned to the July 24 downside analog (Block C). After the mixed 08:30 ET Producer Price Index release on November 13, 2026, SOXL briefly rose to 66.82 before giving back most of that move. In regular trading, it broke below 62.45-62.40, reached 52.361, and closed at 58.320 (-11.00%). SOXS reached 54.940 and closed at 50.780 (+11.07%). The paper also reviews a 200-share SOXS trade that earned USD 20.00 gross before costs. The paper proposes operationally testable triggers for the Monday, November 16, 2026 session. The evidence remains exploratory and does not establish that pre-market microstructure generally dominates macroeconomic releases.

title: Steady States Exist Because the Economy Is Unstable for Households: Collective Fear and Economic Depressions

detail.title: Steady States Exist Because the Economy Is Unstable for Households: Collective Fear and Economic Depressions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the origin of a steady state is driven not by impatience, but by households' anxiety about future economic instability. Traditional models assume that a steady state exists because expected utilities are discounted by a constant rate of time preference (RTP). However, empirical evidence shows that the RTP is not temporally constant, generating a time-inconsistency problem. This paper proposes that households' anxiety about future instability-trather than impatience-enables a steady state to realize. Under this instability, households face a risk of incurring large debts that can subsequently be forgiven. Anticipating this risk, households bring forward their consumption, which paradoxically sustains a steady state. Since the steady state is driven by consumer confidence, it can experience significant fluctuations, and widespread fear can trigger a severe economic downturn.

title: AI and Firm Location Choice: Experimental and Field Evidence

detail.title: AI and Firm Location Choice: Experimental and Field Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Firms increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) where to locate. This paper audits that advice with a blind-versus-label experiment: an LLM ranks five Chinese cities that have identical stated fundamentals, and the only difference between conditions is whether real city names or anonymous labels are shown. Across 9,644 trials and seventeen models, revealing names moves Tier-1 cities down by 0.46 rank positions and moves lower-tier cities up. A tier-only condition, which shows the commercial tier without the name, reproduces the effect, so it operates at the category level. The effect is near zero for reasoning models and large for several standard ones, and it widens the expected gap to the profit-maximizing choice by 5.2 percentage points of the withintrial profit spread. Real city data then show that tier adds nothing for manufacturing output, GDP, house prices, or manufacturing entry once the stated fundamentals are controlled, but it predicts population and all-sector firm entry, and among Tiers 2 to 4 realized entry rises with tier while the AI's adjustment falls. The audit identifies a causal label dependence; it does not by itself separate a stereotype from a legitimate prior.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical and empirical framework to analyze China's interest rate corridor, focusing on the Lending Facility (LF) instrument rate. We employ a financial accelerator model featuring an explicit corridor and a novel accessibility cost (α), which captures implicit costs during LF application. The theoretical properties of the model explain key stylized facts associated with the corridor operation. The study highlights several fundamental properties of the corridor as a policy framework: (1) Width of corridor is an active policy tool, implying that LF and deposit facility (DF) policies should be designed cohesively within a unified corridor framework; (2) Corridor policy efficiency varies with the level of market liquidity; and (3) Market rate usually resides above the mid-point of the corridor due to structural liquidity condition. Empirically, we employ the Joint Power Prior (JPP) Bayesian estimation to quantify the α time series, identifying structural breakpoints that align with major policy and market events. The estimated model simulates market dynamics that conform to all typical facts. This study provides a quantitative tool for monitoring LF transmission efficiency.

detail.abstract: We study how financial distress affects the reallocation of scientific human capital and innovation beyond distressed firms. Combining confidential U.S. Census employer-employee records with firm financial information, R&D surveys, and inventorlevel patent data, we find that firms facing greater refinancing pressure disproportionately lose scientifically oriented inventors. At potential destination firms, incumbent inventors with greater predetermined exposure to reallocating scientific talent, based on geographic proximity and technological similarity, exhibit higher subsequent patent productivity. The increase in patenting is disproportionately concentrated in inventions citing knowledge developed by scientifically oriented inventors at financially vulnerable firms. Greater exposure is also associated with increased science-linked patenting, particularly among development-oriented incumbent inventors. Together, our findings suggest that financial distress reshapes the allocation of scientific expertise across firms, facilitating the diffusion and application of scientific knowledge in subsequent innovation.

title: The Onion Without a Core: Cultural Authenticity and the Governance Gaps Exposed by the Tabung Haji RCI

detail.title: The Onion Without a Core: Cultural Authenticity and the Governance Gaps Exposed by the Tabung Haji RCI

This research was conducted independently and solely for academic and professional purposes.

detail.abstract:
Purpose — This paper examines a paradox at Lembaga Tabung Haji, Malaysia's Islamic pilgrimage
fund: employees consistently describe a warm, Shariah-consistent workplace, yet the declassified
Royal Commission of Inquiry report documents systemic governance failure, creative accounting, and
losses exceeding RM12 billion. The paper asks how a supportive operational culture can coexist with
governance-level ethical failure, and what this reveals about the relationship between employee
experience and ethical accountability.

Design/methodology/approach — A theory-informed single-case study using documentary and
secondary evidence: the RCI report, parliamentary statements, the institution's integrity architecture,
employee review data, and corroborating internal survey findings. Hofstede's onion model is applied
critically to read formal cultural signals against evidence of enacted conduct.

Findings — The observable cultural layers—symbols and rituals—were authentic and experienced as
such, whereas the values layer, which requires leadership accountability, was not. The paper develops
the concept of layered authenticity to describe this asymmetry. Cultural warmth at the operational level
did not function as a safeguard at the governance level; safeguards were overridden precisely where
authority to override them resided.

Originality/value — The paper challenges the assumption that espoused values, employee
satisfaction, and ethical climate are convergent indicators of organisational health. It argues that
organisational culture should be assessed at the layer where consequential decisions are made, not only
where most people work, and sets out structural constraints designed to remove the authority to
override.

title: The Traffic Warden's Dilemma, Deterrence Paradoxes, and Spatio-Temporal Structure

detail.title: The Traffic Warden's Dilemma, Deterrence Paradoxes, and Spatio-Temporal Structure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We formalize the tripartite strategic interaction-among a street-level traffic enforcement officer, an alleged offender, and a revenue-maximizing municipal agency-establishing "The Traffic Warden's Dilemma". Grounded in non-cooperative game theory and mechanism design, the model examines the roadside encounter in which the officer manages discourse and temporal friction to extract an illicit bribe while deliberately evading explicit criminal liability. We analytically prove the punitive deterrence paradox: under weak internal monitoring, raising statutory fines fails to deter violations; it merely expands the bilateral bargaining surplus and inflates equilibrium roadside rents. Introducing continuous audiovisual surveillance via body-worn cameras (BWC) exposes a second structural anomaly: the hypersurveillance paradox. Because technical monitoring penalizes visible acts of commission (accepting a bribe) while remaining blind to discretionary omission ("wave-through" enforcement), officers retreat into strategic bureaucratic passivity. The ensuing citizen impunity and municipal revenue collapse force the regulatory principal into an endogenous institutional relaxation, loosening camera oversight while imposing coercive minimum citation quotas. Finally, contrasting this finite roadside encounter against the infinite-horizon administrative extraction loop ("the runaround"), we derive the rational time-truncation theorem, whose structural isomorphisms extend across tax audits, customs inspection, financial supervision, asymmetrical warfare in eroded states, and corporate holdups .

title: Online Network Revenue Management with Delayed and Composite Demand Feedback
affiliations: Zhejiang University - School of Management, National University of Singapore (NUS) and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Online Network Revenue Management with Delayed and Composite Demand Feedback
detail.abstract: We study online network revenue management when pricing decisions generate demand that is realized over several periods. Observed sales combine purchases from multiple past decisions, complicating learning and resource control. We develop two primal-dual policies that separate feedback for action learning, resource-price updates, and capacity accounting. Under stationary stochastic demand with attributable feedback, Estimated-Mean Primal-Dual (EM-PD) decouples delayed learning from timely resource control through estimates of current-action consumption. For K actions over T periods with maximum lag L, EM-PD achieves ︁ O(√ KT + K(L + 1)) regret relative to the optimal dynamic policy, preserving the standard learning rate with an additive delay penalty. Under adversarial demand with composite anonymous feedback, Randomized Temporal Isolation Primal-Dual (RTI-PD) coordinates learning and control through randomized blocks, obtaining action-consistent feedback without restoring attribution. RTI-PD guarantees a ρ fraction of the resource-relaxed best fixed action in hindsight, up to an additive O(√︁ (L + 1)KT + L + 1) loss, where ρ is the capacity-to-horizon ratio. Both policies maintain pathwise feasibility. Numerical experiments show EM-PD remains effective across different purchase timings and capacity levels, and RTI-PD outperforms an aggregate-feedback baseline despite fewer updates.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to create measurable productive capacity across healthcare, and recent estimates place the annual net value of full adoption in the hundreds of billions of dollars. Notwithstanding that promise, realizing the value depends on organizational change as much as on technology. In this working paper, I argue that the decisive variable is the Decision Layer: the institutional capability between technological output and enterprise consequence, through which leaders determine where automation belongs, how performance is validated, and how released capacity is redeployed. I propose a seven-step Productivity Realization Framework that traces each AI-enabled improvement from work eliminated and time released, through capacity created and redeployed, to economic and patient results, with governance that makes the gains recur. The care of chronically critically ill patients, which crosses organizational boundaries and links referral acceptance, staffing, documentation, reimbursement, and quality, serves as the most demanding proving ground for the discipline. I also introduce the LEAD profile, an organization's standing on the measures an accountable care organization is paid on, which Working Paper No. 2 develops. The paper concludes with a research agenda that includes a national AI Productivity Realization Index and an annual report.

detail.abstract: We replay the 155,534 analysed invoice clearings of a real purchase-to-pay event log (BPI Challenge 2019) through a deterministic min() gate of seven predicates declared before the data were read, over the evidence reconstructed from the log at clearing time. 17,748 clearings (11.41%, 95% interval [10.94%, 11.92%]) were made on evidence that failed at least one predicate, carrying 19.41% of the cleared value [16.04%, 23.09%]. Most fail D4 with the line's creation as the last approval-bearing event; counting only changes after an explicit approval (exploratory), exposure is 0.90% of clearings and 5.65% of value. Clearings with an absent or late goods receipt were followed by a corrective event within 60 days at 5.64% against 0.93% (Holm-adjusted p = 4.53e-4); clearings after a change of price or quantity since approval at 1.91% against 0.96% (p = 3.48e-7). On a registered sample, two model families shown the ERP view held 100.0% and 99.6% of lines with a failed predicate and 53.0% and 57.3% of clean lines; people, measured as non-release within 60 days, held 33.0% and 34.0%; the gate holds the first and allows the second by construction. Paper 5's compiler, given three declared losses, does not reproduce the registered contract in any category. A coverage matrix states which defect classes the log cannot expose; the authority class has zero incidence. Preregistered, every number from a committed result file, reproduced externally. No causal claim is made.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports organisational decision-making, yet it is up to human users to evaluate AI advice. Prior work highlights cognitive and emotional factors, but less is known about how workflow design shapes advice utilisation in repeated interactions with fallible systems. We examine two design levers, advice placement (AI-First vs. Human-First) and an overall accuracy warning, and analyse how they influence utilisation and its cognitive drivers. Using a forecasting task, we conduct a laboratory experiment that systematically manipulates these levers and captures behavioural and cognitive responses across repeated decisions. Our results show that advice placement shapes self-and systemevaluations, directly reduces advice utilisation, and has implications for task engagement. An overall accuracy warning, in contrast, impacts system perception but is not sufficient to alter behaviour and does not produce caution. Moreover, a user's baseline capability for the task is predictive of system evaluation and responses to faulty advice.

detail.abstract: The Mobile banking agent operations have emerged as a critical enabler of financial inclusion across rural and peri-urban communities in Uganda. Karenga District, a remote administrative unit in Kaabong District, Karamoja sub-region, exemplifies the challenges and opportunities inherent in extending financial services to underserved populations through mobile agent operations networks. Despite the socioeconomic promise of these services, the proliferation of mobile devices used by banking agents introduces a complex attacks of cybersecurity vulnerabilities that remain inadequately assessed and poorly managed. This study designed and validates a comprehensive Cybersecurity Threat Assessment Framework (CTAF) tailored specifically to the operational context of mobile banking agents in Karenga District. Drawing on a mixed quantitative and qualitative study design informed by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), CIA triads, the Routine Activity Theory (RAT), and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the study examines the nature, frequency, and impact of cyber threats affecting the mobile banking agents, with emphasis on device-level vulnerabilities, social engineering attacks, SIM-swap fraud, man-in-the-middle interception, and inadequate security practices. Primary data were collected through a questionnaire survey and semi-structured interviews with total number of respondents 100 mobile banking agents, 10 banking representatives staff from financial service providers, and 10 frequent mobile banking customers. Thematic analysis and cross-case synthesis were employed to derive patterns, relationships, and theoretical propositions. The Findings of this study indicate that mobile banking agents in Karenga District operate within a high-risk cybersecurity environment characterized by weak password hygiene, absence of multifactor authentication, inadequate endpoint security, limited cybersecurity literacy, and systemic gaps in regulatory oversight. Therefore, this study informs about a comprehensive Cybersecurity Threats Assessment Framework tailored to the mobile agents' banking operations in rural areas like Karenga District and comprising five interlinked components: Threat Identification, Vulnerability Assessment, Risk Prioritization, Control Recommendations, and Monitoring and Review. The framework offers actionable guidance for financial institutions, regulators, and policymakers to strengthen cybersecurity governance in last-mile mobile banking operations.

detail.abstract:
One universally established fact is that emotions cannot be dissociated from humans. Workplace activity is planned, assigned and monitored through procedures and performance measures, but people may interpret the same situations differently and experience personality clashes. Recruitment commonly evaluates qualifications, professional experience and skills. These are important indicators of capability, but they do not fully show how a person may apply that capability when dealing with colleagues, pressure, disagreement, recognition, responsibility or authority. This conceptual paper examines what weighs more at work: experience or the personality behind it. Its guiding proposition is that experience may help a person get the job done, while personality-related tendencies, emotional responses, reasoning and observable behavior influence how the work is carried out. 

Activities are monitored, controlled, regulated, while personalities can clash. Workplace conflict may involve personality differences and the emotional responses that arise when people interpret events, feedback, authority or treatment differently. Such responses can influence communication, cooperation and work behavior. However, conflict must also be examined in its organizational context, including perceived unfairness, workload, unclear responsibilities and management practices. The paper examines Emotional Intelligence (EI), personality-related assessment and proposed measures such as psychological counseling, brainstorming and responsible sentiment analysis. It also introduces adaptive Human-AI capability synergy, considering how AI can be useful to individual employees while employees learn to evaluate and benefit from AI. These are proposed areas for organizational practice and empirical study, not established solutions. The discussion is situated within the human-centered perspective of Human Valorizing Concept 5.0.

detail.abstract: Farming households in rural India have to cope with erratic rainfall, crop losses, rising input costs, unstable prices and the paperwork that comes with claiming public support. This paper presents a descriptive survey of 51 respondents from the village of Songao in Satara District, Maharashtra. A structured questionnaire gathered information on respondent background, land and soil, soil testing, irrigation, machinery, awareness and use of government schemes, farming difficulties, selling arrangements, income bands, preferred forms of support and interest in a WhatsApp-based chatbot. Results are reported as counts and percentages. Black soil was the most common soil type (72.5%), and two-thirds of respondents (66.7%) had tested their soil. Drip irrigation was named most often (37.3%), whereas 29.4% relied on rain. Nearly four in five respondents (78.4%) knew of government schemes, yet delays and paperwork headed the list of obstacles among valid answers. Irregular rainfall was the foremost challenge (47.1%), 51.0% had experienced crop failure during the previous two years, and 74.5% were unhappy with the prices they received. Better irrigation was the support most often requested (39.2%). A WhatsApp chatbot was seen as useful by 68.6%, while 29.4% were unsure. The findings apply to this sample alone: how respondents were selected is not recorded, so the results should not be extended to farmers in general without representative research.

detail.abstract: On September 17, 2026, the Anthropic Institute published a prototype R&D Automation Index reporting that Claude leads 26% of a fixed basket of model research and development tasks, using a person-time weighting proxy, as of August 2026. No measured task category was rated fully autonomous (Favaro & Wright, 2026). This essay distinguishes that distribution of automation ratings from research productivity, effective human control, and public factual reliability. It extends the author's Maestro Model from the solitary scholar to the LLM enterprise: named human decision-makers retain responsibility for purpose, permissions, verification, intervention, and acceptance. A review of public evidence from five frontier developers identifies existing safety, evaluation, research, and response functions, including proactive work and selected continuous human escalation. The remaining question is their adequacy, not their existence. Published monitoring and incident records provide partial evidence but do not furnish a comparable account of staffing, residual errors, and accepted outcomes. Explicit 25-, 100-, and 250-person oversight scenarios yield annual cash budgets of approximately $14 million, $57 million, and $147 million; including assumed annual equity compensation raises them to approximately $18 million, $72 million, and $186 million. These are planning scenarios, not disclosed laboratory budgets. Incremental benefit-cost calculations identify break-even reductions in firm losses and user verification time without presuming that additional staff necessarily produce those benefits. The essay situates these findings within Anthropic's financial disclosures, and argues that its public-benefit-corporation form and disclosed propagated-error risk make the adequacy of oversight expenditure a matter of directors' duty of care: under the Court of Chancery's first construction of Delaware's Section 365 balancing mandate (Drakes Landing, 2026) and the Caremark line on mission-critical risk, the board's documented, informed attention to the risk is what protects it, and the proposed disclosure scorecard is that record. The essay closes by arguing for examinable evidence that human authority and verification remain effective as delegation expands.

detail.abstract: Deepfake education is often expected to encourage verification, yet awareness, beliefs about intention and actual checking require different evidence. This study examines these distinctions in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh, including a descriptive subset of 227 law students. The questionnaire separately asks about awareness of convincing AI-generated media, source checking, corroboration, the perceived influence of awareness on verification intention, and intended restraint in sharing unverified material. Responses were analysed using item distributions, joint endorsement, paired comparisons, exploratory rank correlations and threshold sensitivity summaries. Overall, 244 respondents (63.4%) endorsed deepfake awareness, 265 (68.8%) reported source checking, and 278 (72.2%) reported seeking corroboration. The statement that awareness increases verification intention received 327 endorsements (84.9%), exceeding source-checking endorsement by 16.1 percentage points (pointwise bootstrap 95% interval 10.1-21.8). However, awareness had small ordinal correlations with checking and corroboration (ρ = 0.084 and 0.077); neither was statistically distinguishable from zero after adjustment within the four-test family. Law-student summaries showed a similar ordering of endorsement. These findings concern differently worded self-reports and do not establish an intention-behaviour gap, intervention effect or inability to identify deepfakes. The article contributes a measurement-based distinction between endorsing an awareness-to-intention proposition and independently observing verification. It recommends evaluating media-literacy education through source tracing, corroboration and discernment tasks that include authentic as well as manipulated content. Undocumented recruitment and the mixed sample limit population inference.

detail.abstract: This paper presents the design and build plan for the At Home Music Tutor App, a free, offline, deterministic desktop application that listens to a piano or acoustic-guitar student play a piece from sheet music, compares the performance to the score, and produces a saved, constructive written critique for use between lessons with a human music teacher. Version 3 of the combined document revised Version 2 in the light of two independent technical reviews, one by an OpenAI system and one by an Anthropic system, and added a mini-pilot phase in which the complete loop is built and measured on a single short score with one adult student before the five-piece pilot begins. Version 3.1 records the results of the first half of that mini-pilot: a virtual stage in which the assessment engine was built in a model sandbox on two beginner pieces and measured on 480 synthetic cases across four runs, with every issue found, every fix made and every issue remaining logged in appendices, and a protocol issued for an independent parallel run by a second laboratory’s system. Version 3.2 records the outcome of that independent run, in which an OpenAI system reproduced every synthetic result and then found, by constructed counterexamples and a source audit, seven groups of defects in the engine’s decision rules; records the builder’s fifth run, which corrected them and turned the reviewer’s counterexamples into permanent regression tests; writes the contract decisions those findings raised into the specification; and adds the laptop application and the studio test-bed protocol with which the physical half of the mini-pilot begins. Part I, the Prototype Specification, defines the roles of teacher, student, and parent, the inputs, the processing pipeline, six assessment criteria with confidence tiers, two interaction modes (reference playback and guided review), a camera subsystem for guitar, constraints, a phased scope with a mini-pilot, a pilot, and a release inside the first phase, seventeen acceptance criteria with their metrics defined, one authoritative phase-to-criteria table, one test-data protocol, and a risk register. Part II, the Build Plan, identifies the foundational software as a standalone assessment engine, recommends an open-source stack and the research projects to build from, lays out ordered next steps with time gates and a human-effort allowance for the whole project, and assesses which frontier large language model systems are best suited to construct the software. The argument throughout is that a deterministic, local, teacher-subordinate design is not only the safer product for children and families but also the more tractable engineering problem, because it removes the components that are hardest to test. The virtual stage added one method to that argument: the score is treated as the standard trace, the student’s recording is reduced to the same curves on the same beat axis, and the critique’s confidence tiers are computed from graded residuals rather than asserted. The work is presented as a worked example of the Maestro Model, in which the human author retains full intellectual sovereignty over specification and acceptance while directing AI systems as instruments of construction and, in this version, of review.

detail.abstract: The transition to SAP S/4HANA requires organisations to choose how much of their existing enterprise resource planning environment to retain, redesign or selectively transform. Greenfield, Brownfield and selective data transition approaches are frequently discussed as competing migration routes, yet published industry surveys report different preference patterns across periods and respondent populations. This study conducts a descriptive comparative analysis of publicly available aggregate findings from three industry surveys: the PwC-LeanIX study (2018; 134 respondents), the Sogeti State of Worldwide Business Assurance for SAP Solutions study (2023; 501 respondents for the migration-approach question), and Kearney's SAP S/4HANA cloud-transition survey (200 respondents reported in its survey materials). The analysis preserves each survey's original denominator and category definitions and does not pool percentages across studies. Brownfield was the most frequently reported approach in the 2018 PwC-LeanIX and 2023 Sogeti findings, whereas Greenfield was the largest single category in Kearney's more recent planned-migration results. This variation cautions against treating any route as universally preferred or superior. The reports also identify considerations relevant to finance transformation, including process improvement, legacy complexity, data quality, continuity, testing and confidence in business outcomes. However, the reviewed surveys do not provide a harmonised, independently verified measure of finance performance by migration route. The study therefore develops an evidence-informed decision framework linking route selection to process fit, data condition, control requirements, delivery capacity and post-implementation benefits measurement. The findings are descriptive and cannot establish causal relationships between migration route and business value.

detail.abstract: An access decision can cease to apply while its explanation continues to govern an agent's work. We examine this problem in the management of long-term memory for enterprise LLM agents. Drawing on organizational memory, coordination, and data governance, we distinguish the validity of retained facts, the current applicability of access decisions, and the recovery of dependent work. Three computational studies trace these responsibilities through IT-service workflows. Study 1 compares sharing and source maintenance across 1,152 assignments and locates a purpose-transition gap in cross-task working context. Study 2 evaluates authorization and provenance filtering across 768 assignments: enforcing the input boundary can also remove refusal explanations needed by subsequent roles. Study 3 evaluates reusable authority-issued denial receipts across four models and 4,320 assignments. Receipts reduce rejected source queries by 83.5%–86.9%, but aggregate completion conceals concentrated recovery failures. Terra and Gemini complete all authorization-restoration assignments; DeepSeek and Kimi sometimes refuse despite the withdrawal of invalid structured receipts. For Kimi, overall effective completion rises from 268 to 279 of 288 assignments, while restoration-window completion falls from 38 to 32 of 38. Retained explanations preserve the earlier denial without recording its decision dependency; one delivery role even rejects newly authorized evidence obtained upstream. The findings identify dependency coverage as a management requirement for decision reuse. Enterprises need ownership of a decision's current applicability, reassessment of its derived explanations, and transition-specific acceptance tests that connect compliant delivery to acquisition, inference, and maintenance work.

detail.abstract: Despite growing calls for "participatory AI" in response to concerns about bias, labor exploitation, and accountability, participation is often invoked without specifying whether it meaningfully redistributes power. In data annotation, participatory language frequently functions as legitimizing rhetoric, even as authority over problem framing, workflows, and downstream use remains centralized. This paper examines when, and under what conditions, data annotation can be considered genuinely participatory. We present a comparative analysis of six data annotation initiatives across commercial, institutional, and community-governed contexts using an integrative framework that distinguishes between epistemic, procedural, and governance authority in data annotation. Across cases, we identify three recurring configurations of authority in AI data work: managed commercial annotation, institutionalized expert and volunteer contribution, and community-governed annotation. We find that genuine participation does not arise from human involvement, ethical labor conditions, domain expertise, or transparency alone, but emerges where structural conditions redistribute authority over problem framing, annotation practices, and downstream control. We reframe participation as a question of authority distribution and knowledge governance rather than inclusion alone, with implications for data politics and democratic accountability in AI governance.

title: From Data Analysis to Decision: A Four-Factor Framework for Discrepancies and Errors in Indicator Monitoring Systems

detail.title: From Data Analysis to Decision: A Four-Factor Framework for Discrepancies and Errors in Indicator Monitoring Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no conflict of interest for the publication of this.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not have any funding.

detail.abstract: Indicators are often treated as objective summaries of organizational, programmatic, or policy performance, yet every reported value is the final output of an information-production chain that extends from data capture through storage, transformation, updating, analysis, review, and interpretation. This paper develops a four-factor framework for diagnosing discrepancy-generating mechanisms and error risks in indicator monitoring systems. The framework distinguishes (1) input and data-capture disturbances; (2) data-flow and information-system disturbances; (3) temporal-alignment and updating disturbances; and (4) human analytical and review disturbances. Building on data-quality research, information-systems theory, officialstatistics quality frameworks, human-error research, spreadsheet auditing, and performance-measurement literature, the paper formalizes the distinction between an observed discrepancy and a genuine error through the decomposition D = ΔY* + ΔE, where ΔY* represents legitimate change in the reference-correct quantity and ΔE represents error-induced divergence. A Monte Carlo simulation then examines error locus and propagation, temporal discrepancies without error, reporting pressure relative to validation capacity, reviewer misclassification, integrated discrepancy composition, and interactions between input and dataflow disturbances. The simulation shows that disagreement between informational products is an outcome requiring diagnosis rather than direct evidence of error. The framework therefore treats indicator reliability as a property of the entire socio-technical information-production chain and offers a diagnostic sequence for tracing, reproducing, and interpreting discrepancies before corrective action is taken.

detail.abstract: Enterprises increasingly distribute database workloads across cloud providers to meet availability, residency, modernization, and service-specific requirements. This distribution also fractures security evidence: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) and Amazon Web Services (AWS) expose distinct identity models, policy languages, audit streams, encryption services, and managed-database boundaries. This conceptual research paper proposes the Cross-Cloud Database Assurance Fabric (CCDAF), a provider-neutral operating model for connecting identity governance, database security controls, continuous compliance monitoring, and intelligent threat detection without pretending that cloud platforms are interchangeable. CCDAF combines a normalized asset-and-identity graph, provider-native enforcement, a common control ontology, evidence lineage, and a human-governed analytics loop. The paper synthesizes public standards and provider guidance, derives design principles, and presents three explicitly hypothetical enterprise scenarios involving privileged access, configuration drift, and anomalous database activity. It contributes (1) a layered architecture, (2) an identity-and-evidence model that preserves provider semantics, (3) a staged automation policy that separates observation from high-impact enforcement, and (4) a reproducible evaluation agenda. No experiment or production deployment is claimed; all examples are illustrative. The central proposition is that useful AI in multi-cloud database defense should prioritize evidence quality, explainable risk ranking, and safe orchestration over autonomous action. A research agenda proposes measurements for detection quality, control coverage, false-positive burden, evidence completeness, remediation latency, and recovery readiness. The framework is intended to help security, database, platform, audit, and privacy teams coordinate controls across OCI and AWS while retaining human accountability.

detail.abstract: AI and data projects create value only when they change business outcomes: lower costs, faster delivery, better decisions, new revenue, or reduced risk. Yet most organizations still approve these investments on the strength of a technical demonstration and a single ROI estimate, and most published failure statistics suggest the results are poor. Gartner reported that by the end of 2025 at least 50% of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept due to poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs, or unclear business value ([1]), and it forecasts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 ([2]). Meanwhile, organizations estimate that roughly a quarter to a third of all cloud infrastructure spend is wasted ([3]). This paper proposes one common financial framework, built on managerial accounting fundamentals, with different evaluation rules for different project types: cloud migration, existing ML systems, data engineering, BI and analytics, new AI from proof of concept to rollout, and agentic AI. The framework connects full lifecycle costs, measurable benefits, explicit treatment of uncertainty, and accountable business ownership-from the first experiment to ongoing operations. Its practical output is a staged evidence-gate funding model and a one-page executive decision sheet. The paper is presented as a conceptual framework with illustrative applications; all numerical examples are hypothetical and clearly labelled.

detail.abstract: For most of the twentieth century, government policies shielded domestic markets from foreign competition through tariffs, quotas, and import restrictions. Fiscal barriers such as customs tariffs, import licenses, and quantitative restrictions were the foundations of the architecture of international trade, affecting the ability of foreign products to enter particular markets. But with the advent of the modern era of international trade, it is the domestic regulatory institutions that govern trade rather than customs checkpoints. Artificial intelligence is one of these instances. From transparency requirements to risk-classification regimes, from data governance to algorithmic accountability, jurisdictions around the world are taking steps to introduce new, AIspecific regimes. The measures have clearly and unarguably legitimate aims such as consumer protection, national security and fundamental rights. However, they also define who is included and how, in digital markets. Regulatory decisions on the operation of AI within societies will thus be "non-tariff measures (NTMs) that will impact market access for the hyper-specialized AI applications already in use and the many under development," states the Cambridge chapter on artificial intelligence and international economic law. 1 The WTO's 2025 World Trade Report is also in line with this structural shift, highlighting that "AI-enabling goods, including semiconductors, are relatively cheaply traded, yet are subject to many more non-tariff restrictions, such as antidumping duties". Meanwhile, it is noted that "AI-intensive services such as accounting, auditing, insurance, or telecommunications have some of the highest tariff restrictions for mode (crossborder) trade. 2 If market access now depends on satisfying domestic AI regulations rather than paying customs duties, have AI regulations become the twenty-first century's non-tariff barriers?

detail.abstract: Computational psychiatry seeks to connect neurobiological processes, latent cognitive computations, and observable behaviour through generative mathematical models. Adams, Huys, and Roiser (2016) developed an influential conceptual framework connecting hierarchical Bayesian inference, predictive coding, reinforcement learning, dopaminergic signalling, and psychiatric symptoms. However, a unified stochastic treatment of the interaction between hierarchical inference and dopaminergic dynamics, together with rigorous stability and statistical identifiability results, remains an important mathematical direction. We develop a coupled stochastic state-space framework in which latent hierarchical beliefs, prefrontal precision, tonic dopaminergic activity, and phasic dopaminergic activity evolve jointly. The model is formulated as a multidimensional stochastic differential equation with bounded nonlinear coupling and linear dissipative regulation. Our first contribution is a stochastic stability analysis. Under explicit contraction conditions on the coupling matrix, we establish global existence and pathwise uniqueness, exponential contraction of trajectories, existence and uniqueness of an invariant probability measure, and quantitative convergence in Wasserstein distance. We also derive Lyapunov drift bounds and characterise the equilibrium structure of the associated deterministic system. Our second contribution concerns computational regime transitions. We derive a sufficient parameter region in which the deterministic system possesses a unique globally asymptotically stable equilibrium. We then formulate precise Jacobian conditions for detecting loss of stability, saddle-node bifurcations, and Hopf bifurcations outside the contraction region. Our third contribution concerns statistical identifiability. We demonstrate an explicit observational equivalence between prior precision and sensory precision when only posterior means are measured. We show how additional uncertainty measurements and controlled stimulus manipulations can resolve this ambiguity. Finally, under an inverse-Lipschitz identifiability condition and a sub-Gaussian observation model, we derive a finite-sample parameter estimation guarantee. The resulting framework provides a mathematical bridge between stochastic cognitive dynamics, neurocomputational mechanisms, and experimentally distinguishable hypotheses. The model is phenomenological and is not presented as an established biological mechanism. Its neurobiological interpretation requires independent experimental validation.
