title: Strategic Repayment and Latent Fragility in Financial Networks: Why Banks Withhold Payable Liquidity

detail.title: Strategic Repayment and Latent Fragility in Financial Networks: Why Banks Withhold Payable Liquidity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the research reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research is theoretical and does not involve human participants, patient data, animal subjects or identifiable personal information. Accordingly, ethical approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: A network in which every bank pays in full can nevertheless admit a self-fulfilling settlement freeze under the same balance-sheet fundamentals. Thus, observing full repayment does not establish the uniqueness or robustness of the payment equilibrium. We derive this result from a precautionary-liquidity choice: banks may delay otherwise feasible payments to insure an interim funding need, trading a positive settlementdiscipline cost against the marginal value of retained cash. The optimal reserve is a critical quantile of future liquidity requirements, and the repayment rule nests Eisenberg-Noe maximal feasible clearing exactly. Counterparty underpayment both reduces current cash and raises desired reserves. We characterise network amplification and the conditions for coexistence, including a homogeneous two-bank GPD frontier in which interbank exposure and maximum funding pass-through enter through one dimensionless index. A two-date settlement accounting rule distinguishes payment timing from ultimate default. The main result concerns equilibrium coexistence; the conditional best-response adjustment diagnostic does not assign selection probabilities.

title: Simulated Losses, Exchange-App Activity, and Bitcoin Buy-and-Hold: A Methodological Re-Examination of BIS Working Paper No. 1049

detail.title: Simulated Losses, Exchange-App Activity, and Bitcoin Buy-and-Hold: A Methodological Re-Examination of BIS Working Paper No. 1049

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Working Paper No. 1049 (Auer, Cornelli, Doerr, Frost and Gambacorta, 2022; revised July 2023) builds a Sensor Tower panel of retail crypto-exchange app downloads and daily active users (DAUs) for 95 countries from August 2015 to June 2022. Price-led app entry is well documented. The BIS publication page summary states that around three-quarters of users "lost money on their Bitcoin investments", and the PDF introduction (printed p. 3) says "over 75%" and refers to cryptocurrencies. Those figures come from simulations that time Bitcoin purchases to downloads and mark a $100-per-month rule in 2022, after the late-2021 peak. Using the public Group of Twenty (G20) supplement and three public Bitcoin price series, I find buy-and-hold returns of about 69–71× (compound annual growth rate, CAGR, about 84–85%) over the authors' window. Download-weighted dollar-cost averaging (DCA) approximations can reach the paper's 81% loss rate; switching from monthly highs to averages changes that share only slightly. The G20 mean-DAU series has a power-law slope on Bitcoin age of about 7.8 (Bitcoin price-age about 7.3), with China and Japan as regulatory outliers. A slope-consumer price index (CPI) link using World Bank inflation is positive in the full G20 set and disappears without Argentina and Turkey. The entry evidence stands. The three-quarters figure measures a download-timed purchase rule valued in the 2022 drawdown. It is a different quantity from the sample-wide Bitcoin return.

title: From Maturity Model to Computable Index: Design, Specification, and Verification of the Enterprise Coherence GRC Maturity Index

detail.title: From Maturity Model to Computable Index: Design, Specification, and Verification of the Enterprise Coherence GRC Maturity Index

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the principal of Therapia Consult Ltd (United Kingdom) and the originator of the Enterprise Coherence framework and its digital assessment portal, which are used in commercial advisory and assessment services. The EC GRC Maturity Index specified in this paper is part of that framework. No other personal or financial relationships could have influenced, or be perceived to have influenced, this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. No human participants, organisations, or personal data were involved. The evaluation uses a software reference implementation, simulated data, and a synthetic worked example.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Maturity models for governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) are usually published as conceptual frameworks and implemented locally in spreadsheets, so that the same model can yield different scores in different hands. This paper addresses the gap between a maturity model and a maturity index: a fully specified, computable, auditable, and verifiable scoring artefact. Following design science research, we specify the Enterprise Coherence (EC) GRC Maturity Index for implementation in a digital assessment portal. The instrument is a facet design that crosses five governance domains with ten capability dimensions, yielding fifty diagnostic elements. We formalise the scoring rules, including exact rational arithmetic, half-open classification bands, missing-data rules, and versioned scoring profiles; define coherence analytics (a dispersion-based coherence index, gap flags, a formal-enacted decoupling index, a self-assessment calibration gap, and a dimension profile); and present a reference architecture, data model, and application programming interface with assurance controls. We evaluate the artefact with a reference implementation. Property-based testing over 100,000 random assessments found no violations of five formal properties, and boundary tests exposed a display-classification inconsistency that is removed by three-decimal reporting. Monte Carlo analysis shows that random responding produces scores tightly centred on 3.0, that rater leniency of 0.4 scale points raises mean classification error from 8% to 35%, that a ceiling effect depresses classification just above the Level 5 threshold, and that an inflated global selfrating item upgrades the maturity level in about 5% of assessments. The paper contributes a transferable specification method for computable maturity indices and identifies the measurement safeguards they require.

title: Converging for the Wrong Reasons: Suicide Mortality, the Maastricht Criteria and the Measurement of Social Convergence in Europe
affiliations: University of Nicosia and Nottingham Trent University

detail.title: Converging for the Wrong Reasons: Suicide Mortality, the Maastricht Criteria and the Measurement of Social Convergence in Europe

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study is a secondary analysis of publicly available, aggregate country-level data (WHO Europe European Mortality Database, WHO Mortality Database, Eurostat, AMECO and OECD). It involves no human participants, no individual-level data and no case studies, so neither ethics approval nor informed consent was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Rules and indicators steer policy towards what they measure. The Maastricht criteria made nominal convergence the condition for monetary union, and the European Union's later social indicators judge convergence by averages and gaps between member states. Neither asks how gaps close: a gap narrows both when a lagging country improves and when a leading country deteriorates. Using harmonised suicide mortality, a behavioural measure of extreme ill-being, for 17 western European countries over 1980-2023, we split the realised narrowing of every bilateral gap into these two components. Nominal and social convergence were decoupled: bond-yield and fiscal gaps reopened in the euro crisis while suicide dispersion kept falling. Yet a third of the crisis-era narrowing (95 per cent interval 13-62), and 39 per cent between northern and southern euro members, came from rising suicide in countries that had started with low rates, against none in 1999-2007 once a Portuguese coding break is corrected. Aggregate statistics recorded upward convergence. A simple composition measure, computable from existing statistics, would reveal such episodes.
